courseDescription: A comprehensive journey through the fundamental pillars of linear algebra, emphasizing geometric intuition alongside algebraic rigor. This course moves from the basic mechanics of vectors and linear systems to the sophisticated power of Singular Value Decomposition, helping learners develop a robust mental model for transforming and analyzing data in high-dimensional spaces. Through five progressive units, you will master the language of matrices, the geometry of transformations, and the spectral properties of operators, culminating in practical applications for data compression and system modeling.
targetLearner: Learners seeking a conceptual and practical understanding of linear algebra, including students in STEM fields and professionals interested in the mathematical foundations of data science, computer graphics, and engineering.

projects.project_name: Building a Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) Engine
projects.project_description: In this project, you will build a mathematical engine that can understand the conceptual relationship between documents. You will represent text as vectors, transform them into a shared conceptual space using matrix operations, and use Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to perform semantic search and data compression on a small corpus of text.
projects.final_deliverable: A Python-based Document Analysis Tool that processes a text corpus into a term-document matrix, calculates document similarity, and performs low-rank approximation to identify hidden themes.

units.title: Vectors and Linear Systems
units.description: Establish the foundational vocabulary of linear algebra. In this unit, we explore vectors not just as lists of numbers but as geometric arrows in space, forming the basis for understanding how linear equations intersect and define planes, lines, and hyperplanes.

lectures.title: Vectors and Vector Spaces
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the fundamental objects of linear algebra, moving from simple numerical lists to the geometric intuition of space-filling linear combinations.

sessions.title: Vectors, Scalars, and Vector Arithmetic
sessions.description: This session introduces vectors as both ordered lists of numbers and arrows in space, alongside the rules for addition and scalar multiplication. You will learn to perform basic vector operations and visualize their geometric effects, providing the necessary 'atoms' of data representation required for the upcoming image compression project.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome the audience to the fundamental 'atoms' of linear algebra. Begin by framing a vector not just as a mathematical object, but as a dual personality: a precise list of instructions (the computer science view) and a physical arrow (the physicist's view). Explain that while a single number (a scalar) tells us 'how much', a vector tells us 'which way and how far'. Start the whiteboard by drawing a coordinate system and plotting a point, then draw the arrow from the origin. Emphasize that the tail of the vector can technically be anywhere, but we fix it at the origin to define it by its tip. This conceptual anchor is crucial because it transforms a static point into a dynamic displacement.

Transition to the operation of scalar multiplication. Use the whiteboard to show a vector being multiplied by 2, then by 0.5, and finally by -1. Use the term 'scaling' explicitly, as it provides the intuition for what matrices will eventually do. Highlight a common pitfall: students often forget that multiplying by a negative number flips the direction 180 degrees; visualize this as a 'tug-of-war' where the direction reverses but the 'line of action' remains the same. This is the moment to introduce the first practice task: ask the learners to imagine a force pushing an object north at 5 m/s, and then visualize what happens when that force is scaled by -2. This reveals if they understand that scaling affects both magnitude and sense of direction.

Introduce vector addition through the 'Tip-to-Tail' method. On the whiteboard, draw two vectors, 'a' and 'b', and physically move 'b' so its tail sits on the tip of 'a'. Explain that this represents the cumulative effect of two movements or forces. Contrast this with the 'Parallelogram Law' to show that the order of addition (a+b vs b+a) doesn't change the destination, reinforcing the commutative property without just stating a formula. The key takeaway here is that addition is about combining influences to find a net result. Use the 'resultant force' example to bridge the gap between abstract arrows and real-world physics, asking students to calculate the final position of an object acted upon by two different vectors. This exercise is designed to prove that complex motion can be decomposed into simple, independent steps.

Conclude by linking these basic operations to the upcoming course project on image compression. Explain that an image is essentially a massive vector of pixel values. Scalar multiplication allows us to adjust brightness across the whole image, while vector addition could represent layering one image over another. By mastering these 'atomic' operations, the students are actually learning how to manipulate high-dimensional data. This forward-looking connection ensures the lecture feels like the start of a practical journey rather than a dry arithmetic lesson. Finalize the session by stressing that every complex structure we build later—span, basis, and even SVD—relies entirely on these two simple acts: scaling and adding.

tasks: Represent a physical displacement as a 2D vector.
Calculate the resultant vector of two combined forces.
Visualize scalar multiplication as stretching or flipping a vector arrow.

sessions.title: Linear Combinations and Span
sessions.description: This session explores the concept of scaling and adding vectors to reach new points in space, formally defined as the span. You will learn how to determine if a specific point can be reached by a set of vectors, which is the first step in understanding how data can be reconstructed from basic building blocks.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the simple arithmetic of vectors and the concept of space-filling capabilities. The core mission of this session is to move the learner from 'doing math to a vector' to 'exploring the reach of vectors.' I will start by framing the 'Linear Combination' not as a formula, but as a set of instructions: if vector A is a step forward and vector B is a step to the right, how many different places can we reach by mixing these steps? This sets the stage for thinking about vectors as building blocks rather than just arrows.

To solidify the idea of a linear combination, I will draw two vectors, v and w, on the whiteboard. I'll demonstrate that by varying the scalars (the 'weights') attached to them, we are essentially building a recipe. The most important point here is the word 'combination'—it implies a synthesis. I’ll address a common misconception early: learners often think they can only use positive whole numbers as weights. I will explicitly show how using zero 'collapses' a dimension and how negative weights allow us to move in the opposite direction, creating a full range of motion.

Next, I introduce the 'Span' as the collection of all possible results from these recipes. This is a critical pivot from a single calculation to a set of possibilities. To visualize the span of two vectors in 3D space, I’ll use the analogy of a laser pointer hitting a wall. If we have two vectors pointing in different directions, their span is like an infinite sheet of paper passing through the origin. I want the learners to 'feel' the flatness of that plane. If a third vector (a target) lies on that sheet, it is 'in the span'; if it pokes out of the sheet, it is unreachable. This geometric intuition is vital because it explains why some data can be represented by a model and some cannot.

I will then transition to a practice moment where we test if a target vector lies in the span. Instead of just jumping into row reduction (which comes later), we will use algebraic substitution. This forces the learner to grapple with the underlying logic: 'Can I find two numbers, x and y, that satisfy this equation?' This reveals whether the target vector is redundant or truly unique. If they find no solution, they should realize the target is 'outside' the world created by the original vectors.

Finally, I will wrap up by connecting this to our larger goal of image compression. I’ll explain that in data science, we often try to represent a complex signal (the target vector) as a span of simpler, more efficient basis vectors. If a piece of data is in the span of our chosen 'building blocks,' we can store it using just a few weights rather than the whole dataset. This provides the 'why' behind the 'how,' ensuring the learner sees the span not just as a geometric plane, but as a space of representable information.

tasks: Determine if a target vector lies in the span of two given 3D vectors.
Sketch the span of two non-collinear vectors in 3D space.
Write a vector as a linear combination of others using algebraic substitution.

sessions.title: Linear Independence
sessions.description: This session defines what it means for a set of vectors to be redundant or 'independent'. You will learn to identify when a vector adds new 'information' to a set, a concept that is vital for efficient data compression where we aim to remove redundant information.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by reframing our previous discussion on Span through the lens of 'information efficiency.' If the Span is the territory we can reach, Linear Independence is the question of whether we are carrying unnecessary baggage to get there. I want to start by asking the audience: 'If I give you three directions to travel, but one of those directions can be perfectly described by combining the other two, do you actually have three directions, or just two?' This bridges the geometric intuition they've built with the rigorous need for data compression—if a vector doesn't add a new dimension to our Span, it is redundant. This 'redundancy' is the heart of linear dependence.

To formalize this, I will move to the whiteboard to derive the technical definition. Instead of just stating the equation for a trivial solution, I will present it as a challenge: can we find a way to make a non-zero combination of our vectors equal to the zero vector? I'll write out $c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + ... + c_nv_n = 0$. The 'aha!' moment for the student should be that if any $c$ is non-zero, then at least one vector can be 'blamed' for the others, meaning it can be isolated and expressed as a combination of the rest. I must explicitly warn against the common misconception that 'independence' means the vectors are at right angles (orthogonality); I will clarify that independence only requires that they don't lie in each other's 'shadows' (spans).

Next, we will transition into a visualization exercise using 3D space. I'll sketch two vectors that form a plane. Then, I’ll draw a third vector. If that third vector lies flat on that same plane, it’s dependent—it adds no 'height' or new information. If it points even slightly out of that plane, the set becomes independent. This is a crucial pivot for the project: in image compression, we look for these 'flat' or nearly flat vectors because they represent data that can be discarded without losing the essence of the image. I will ask the students to mentally test a set where one vector is exactly twice another; seeing that $2v_1 - v_2 = 0$ makes the dependence immediately tangible.

Finally, we address the 'Trivial Solution' requirement as the ultimate litmus test. We will walk through a numerical example where we set up a system of equations to solve for the constants. The goal here isn't just calculation, but realizing that if the only way to reach the origin is by 'doing nothing' (setting all constants to zero), the vectors are truly unique contributors to the space. I'll conclude by challenging them to find the redundant vector in a set of three vectors where the third is clearly the sum of the first two, forcing them to see the hidden relationships that lead to dependence before we move on to defining the 'minimal' sets known as Bases.

tasks: Check a set of vectors for linear independence using the definition of trivial solutions.
Identify the redundant vector in a linearly dependent set.
Relate linear independence to the geometric concept of 'not lying in the same line or plane'.

sessions.title: Basis and Dimension
sessions.description: This session synthesizes span and independence to define a basis, the minimal set of vectors that describes a space. You will learn how to calculate the dimension of a subspace, allowing you to quantify the complexity of the datasets you will handle in later units.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing this session as the grand synthesis of everything we have built so far. I will tell the students that if Span represents the reach of our tools and Linear Independence represents the efficiency of our tools, then a 'Basis' is the perfect toolkit—it has exactly what you need to reach everything, with no extra baggage. I’ll draw two non-collinear vectors in 3D space on the whiteboard and ask: 'Do these fill the room?' When they say no, I’ll add a third vector that is a combination of the first two and ask: 'Did that help?' This visualization immediately distinguishes between 'enough vectors' and 'the right vectors.'

Transitioning to the formal definition, I will define a Basis as a set of vectors that is both linearly independent and spans the space. This is the 'Goldilocks' zone of linear algebra. I’ll explain that a basis is the coordinate system’s DNA. To make this concrete, I will contrast the standard unit vectors (i, j) with a slanted, non-orthogonal set of vectors. I’ll show that while both can describe any point in the plane, the standard basis is just the most 'polite' version. The key takeaway here is that while a space has infinitely many bases, they all share a fundamental property: the number of vectors in them. This leads us directly to the concept of Dimension.

To prevent the common misconception that 'dimension' is just about the number of slots in a vector (the ambient space), I will use the example of a 2D plane sitting inside a 3D room. I’ll challenge the class: 'If we are living on this flat sheet of paper floating in the air, how many coordinates do we need to locate ourselves relative to the sheet's corner?' This helps them realize that the dimension of a subspace is defined by the number of vectors in its basis, not by the length of the column vectors themselves. We will walk through an algebraic check where we take three vectors in R^3, find that one is a sum of the others, and conclude that they form a 2D basis for a plane, despite existing in 3D space.

For the practice phase, we will pivot to 'Basis Verification.' I will provide a set of three vectors and ask the students to prove if they form a basis for R^3. This requires them to check for independence (usually via a system of equations or a quick look for proportionality) and then realize that in R^3, if you have three independent vectors, they automatically span the space. This 'counting' shortcut is a major 'aha!' moment for learners. I will then have them find a basis for a specific plane, forcing them to select two independent vectors that satisfy the plane's equation, which reinforces the application of these abstract rules to geometric constraints.

Finally, I will connect this to our upcoming project on image compression. I’ll explain that an image is essentially a high-dimensional vector. Compression is the art of finding a 'better basis'—one where only a few vectors (the most important ones) are needed to reconstruct the 'span' of the image. By the end of this session, students should see a basis not as a math homework requirement, but as a lean, mean representation of data. I’ll wrap up by emphasizing that Dimension is the 'true size' of information, regardless of the container it’s in.

tasks: Verify if a given set of vectors forms a basis for R^2 or R^3.
Find a basis for a plane defined by two vectors.
Determine the dimension of a space based on the number of vectors in its basis.

lectures.title: Systems of Linear Equations
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on the algorithmic process of solving linear equations by organizing data into matrices and applying systematic row operations.

sessions.title: Linear Systems and Augmented Matrices
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to translate a system of linear equations into a compact matrix format. You will learn to use augmented matrices to represent constraints, simplifying complex word problems into a standard mathematical form that computers can solve efficiently.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the first true mechanical step of our linear algebra journey. Today, we move from the conceptual beauty of vectors to the pragmatic reality of solving systems. The primary goal is to convince you that a 'system of linear equations' is not just a list of algebra problems, but a structured data object. We begin by visualizing a simple 2D intersection of lines. I want you to imagine two constraints—perhaps budget and time—crossing at a single point. This physical intersection is our solution. However, as we scale to three, four, or a hundred variables, drawing lines becomes impossible. This is why we need the matrix: a way to strip away the 'noise' of variables like x, y, and z, leaving only the 'signal'—the coefficients.

Let’s start the translation process on the board. I will write a standard 3x3 system, purposely keeping the alignment of variables slightly messy. I'll then demonstrate how the 'augmented matrix' acts as a specialized container for this system. The vertical bar inside the matrix is a crucial visual cue; it represents the equals sign, separating the 'rules' (coefficients) from the 'results' (constants). The key insight here is that the position of a number in the matrix conveys its identity. A number in the first column is implicitly tied to our first variable. By removing the letters, we aren't losing information; we are organizing it for algorithmic processing. A common pitfall for learners is forgetting to include a '0' when a variable is missing from an equation. I will emphasize that a blank space in a system is actually a weight of zero, and skipping this zero in the matrix would shift the entire logical structure of the problem.

Now, let's look at this through the lens of a real-world constraint. Imagine we are managing a factory that produces three types of products, each requiring different amounts of labor, electricity, and raw materials. Each row of our matrix represents a 'resource limit' or a budget constraint, while each column represents a specific 'product.' This shift in perspective is vital: a row is a single rule, while a column is the 'signature' of a variable across all rules. We will pause here for a brief task where you convert a word problem about nutritional requirements into an augmented matrix. This exercise isn't just about syntax; it’s about recognizing that the matrix is a map of dependencies.

Finally, I want to address why we use this format specifically for computers. If you were to tell a computer to 'solve for x,' it wouldn't know where to start. But if you give it an array of numbers, it can perform repetitive arithmetic at lightning speed. We are essentially 'packaging' our problem into a format that leads directly into the Gaussian elimination algorithm we will cover next. I’ll conclude by showing a 'reverse translation'—taking a dense matrix and rebuilding the algebraic equations from it. This ensures you understand that the relationship is bidirectional: the matrix is the math, and the math is the matrix.

tasks: Convert a 3x3 system of equations into an augmented matrix.
Write down the system of equations corresponding to a given augmented matrix.
Interpret the rows and columns of a matrix in the context of a real-world constraint problem.

sessions.title: Gaussian Elimination and Row Echelon Form
sessions.description: This session introduces the Gaussian elimination algorithm to transform matrices into Row Echelon Form. You will learn the mechanics of row swapping, scaling, and addition, mastering the primary tool used for solving systems of equations throughout this course.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the heart of computational linear algebra. Today, we move from just looking at matrices as static grids of numbers to treating them as active objects we can manipulate. Our goal is to master Gaussian Elimination, the universal engine for solving linear systems. I want to frame this not as a set of arbitrary rules, but as a quest for 'mathematical clarity'—taking a cluttered, intertwined system of equations and systematically peeling away the layers until the answer is obvious. We start by establishing the three 'legal moves' we can perform on a matrix: swapping rows, scaling a row by a non-zero constant, and adding a multiple of one row to another. The crucial intuition to emphasize here is that these operations are 'information-preserving'; they change the appearance of the system without changing the intersection points (the solution set) of the underlying lines or planes.

Let’s begin the 'Elimination' process. I’ll start with a messy 3x3 system and demonstrate how we target the first column to create a 'pivot'—our anchor point. I like to describe the pivot as a lighthouse that guides the elimination of everything beneath it. The biggest trap for learners here is arithmetic fatigue. I will pause to show that we aren't just doing math; we are creating zeros. Zero is our best friend in linear algebra because it represents the absence of a variable in a specific equation, which is exactly what 'solving' means. We will focus on transforming the matrix into Row Echelon Form (REF), which looks like a staircase. I’ll draw a staircase over the matrix to show how each row starts with more zeros than the one above it, highlighting that this structure represents a hierarchy of information where the last equation is the simplest to solve.

Once we reach this 'staircase' shape, we need to talk about the 'pivots'—the leading non-zero entries in each row. I’ll explain that pivots are the 'independent variables' that hold the system together. If a column has no pivot, it signals a deeper geometric property we will explore later, but for now, we identify them as the drivers of the solution. A common point of confusion is what happens when a pivot position naturally becomes zero during the process. I’ll demonstrate the 'Row Swap' as a tactical maneuver to keep the elimination engine running, preventing the 'division by zero' error that haunts both students and computer algorithms alike.

Finally, we will perform 'Back-Substitution'. Now that the matrix is in REF, the bottom row usually gives us the value of one variable directly (e.g., 2z = 4). We then plug this value into the row above it, moving up the staircase. This is the moment where the abstract matrix turns back into concrete answers. To solidify this, I'll have the class perform a 'Check' exercise: take the resulting vector and plug it back into the original, messy equations. This reveals the magic of the process—that despite all the swapping and scaling, the fundamental relationship between the variables remained untouched. This session isn't just about getting the right answer; it's about building the muscle memory for the algorithm that powers everything from GPS systems to structural engineering simulations.

tasks: Perform row operations to bring a 3x4 matrix to Row Echelon Form.
Identify pivot positions and pivot columns in a matrix.
Solve a system of equations using back-substitution after reaching echelon form.

sessions.title: Free Variables and Parametric Solutions
sessions.description: This session covers systems with infinitely many solutions by identifying free variables. You will learn to express the entire set of solutions in parametric vector form, which is essential for understanding the 'flexibility' or 'null space' of a linear system.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the previous session's focus on finding a single 'point' solution. I want to frame the idea of 'free variables' not as a failure of the system to produce an answer, but as a description of 'freedom' or 'flexibility' within a geometric space. On the whiteboard, I will start with a simple system in Reduced Row Echelon Form (RREF) where one column lacks a pivot. I will explain that the variables corresponding to pivot columns are 'dependent'—they are locked into place by the others—while the variables without pivots are 'free' to be anything. This distinction is the core of understanding why some systems describe lines or planes rather than just points.

Next, I will guide the transition from the RREF equations to the parametric vector form. This is a critical pedagogical bridge. I will demonstrate how to solve for the pivot variables in terms of the free variables, and then show the 'unbundling' process: splitting the solution vector into a constant vector plus a linear combination of vectors scaled by those free variables. I will emphasize that the free variables now act as 'parameters' (like time or distance along a path). This reveals the 'DNA' of the solution set—it shows that the solutions aren't just a list of numbers, but a structured geometric object like a line or a plane passing through space. This step is vital for preventing the common misconception that 'infinitely many solutions' means 'any random numbers work'; we must show that the solutions are restricted to a very specific, infinite path.

To solidify this, I will introduce a 3-variable example where two variables are free. I will ask the students to visualize what happens when we change one parameter while keeping the other fixed. This helps them 'see' the construction of a plane in 3D space. I will address a frequent point of confusion: the choice of which variable is free. While we usually pick the ones without pivots, I will explain that 'freedom' is a property of the system's dimensionality, not just which column we happen to label. This prepares them for the more abstract concept of the 'null space' later in the course by framing these parametric vectors as the 'directions' in which you can move without breaking the system's constraints.

Finally, the session will conclude with a hands-on exercise where learners must convert a RREF matrix into its parametric vector form and then identify the geometric shape it represents. This exercise is designed to reveal whether students understand the link between the number of free variables and the dimension of the solution set (e.g., 1 free variable = line, 2 free variables = plane). I will wrap up by highlighting that the zero vector is always part of the 'homogenous' version of these solutions, a hint at the subspace structures we will explore in future units.

tasks: Identify free variables from a matrix in Reduced Row Echelon Form.
Write the general solution of a system in parametric vector form.
Distinguish between a unique solution and a solution set representing a line or plane.

sessions.title: Rank, Consistency, and the Number of Solutions
sessions.description: This session explains how to determine if a solution even exists and how many there are based on the rank of the matrix. You will learn to use the Rouché-Capelli theorem to predict system behavior, ensuring you can identify unsolvable or redundant systems in engineering applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the ultimate goal of solving any linear system: knowing whether a solution even exists and, if it does, how many versions of the truth we are dealing with. Start by drawing three simple geometric scenarios on the whiteboard—two lines crossing at a point, two lines being perfectly parallel, and two lines sitting right on top of one another. This visual hook grounds the abstract concepts of 'Unique', 'None', and 'Infinite' in physical space. The key idea here is that we are no longer just 'doing' Gaussian elimination; we are interpreting the 'residue' left behind after the elimination process is complete.

Introduce the concept of 'Rank' as the fundamental measure of information within a matrix. On the whiteboard, show a matrix in row echelon form and circle the pivots. Explain that rank is simply the count of these pivots—the number of 'independent directions' or 'useful pieces of data' the system provides. It is vital to emphasize that the rank tells us how much 'work' the equations are doing. A common pitfall for students is confusing the number of rows with the rank; prevent this by showing a 3x3 matrix where the third row is all zeros, proving that even with three equations, we might only have a rank of two because one equation was redundant.

Next, we bridge the gap between the coefficient matrix (A) and the augmented matrix (A|b) using the Rouché-Capelli Theorem. This is the 'Logic Gate' of linear algebra. Explain that if adding the result vector 'b' increases the rank of the matrix, we have a contradiction—essentially, the system is trying to reach a point in space that its internal 'gears' (the columns of A) cannot reach. Draw a row on the board like [0 0 0 | 5] to symbolize this impossibility. This moment is crucial because it teaches learners to stop calculating and start diagnosing: if the rank of the augmented matrix is greater than the rank of the coefficient matrix, the system is inconsistent, and we can stop searching for a solution immediately.

To wrap up, move into the predictive power of rank regarding the number of solutions. If the system is consistent, we compare the rank to the number of variables (n). If rank equals n, every variable is 'locked' by a pivot, leading to a unique solution. If rank is less than n, we have 'freedom'—the free variables we discussed in the previous session. I will use a simple example of two equations with three variables to show that we are 'short on info,' which naturally creates a line or plane of solutions. The final practice task should involve presenting a matrix and asking learners to predict the outcome before solving it. This reinforces the intuition that the architecture of the matrix—its rank and consistency—determines the destiny of the system long before we reach the final answer.

tasks: Determine the rank of a matrix by counting pivots.
Check the consistency of an augmented matrix.
State the number of solutions (0, 1, or infinity) based on rank and the number of variables.

lectures.title: Geometry of Linear Systems
lectures.description: This lecture bridges the gap between algebraic solutions and their geometric interpretations in high-dimensional space.

sessions.title: Lines, Planes, and Hyperplanes
sessions.description: This session visualizes linear equations as geometric objects where solutions are intersections. You will learn how equations in R^n define hyperplanes, allowing you to visualize the constraints of a linear system as physical barriers in space.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the geometric heart of linear algebra. Today, we shift our focus from the 'how' of solving equations to the 'where' they live. We begin by visualizing a single linear equation as a geometric constraint. In 2D, we know $ax + by = c$ is a line; in 3D, $ax + by + cz = d$ is a plane. The big conceptual leap for this session is understanding that an equation is not just a calculation, but a 'physical barrier' or a slice through space. I will start on the whiteboard by drawing a 3D coordinate system and shading a plane. The key takeaway here is that every point on that surface satisfies the equation. This sets the stage for thinking about higher dimensions: we call these 'hyperplanes' because they generalize the idea of a flat surface into $n$-dimensional space.

Next, we explore what happens when we introduce a second equation. Geometrically, this is where two planes meet. I will illustrate two pieces of paper intersecting in the air. The most common result is a line, which represents the shared solutions between the two constraints. However, I will pause here to address a common misconception: students often assume two planes always intersect in a line. I'll draw two parallel planes to show that 'no solution' isn't just an algebraic result—it's a geometric state where the barriers never touch. This visualization is crucial because it helps learners internalize why we sometimes find ourselves with an empty solution set during Gaussian elimination.

When we move to a system of three equations in 3D, the complexity peaks. I will draw three planes and ask the class to visualize how they might interact. This is the perfect moment for a practice exercise: sketching the intersection. The goal is to see that for a unique solution to exist, all three surfaces must meet at a single, precise point. I’ll then describe the 'failed' scenarios—like three planes forming a triangular prism shape where they intersect in pairs but never all three at once. This explains the geometric reason why a system can be inconsistent even if its parts look fine individually. It's not about the equations being 'wrong'; it's about their physical orientations in space being incompatible.

Finally, we will bridge the gap to the algebraic definition of a plane using a normal vector. I will draw a vector $\mathbf{n}$ sticking straight out of a whiteboard-drawn plane and show that every vector lying within the plane is perpendicular to that normal vector. By using the dot product formula $\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - 	ext{point}) = 0$, we derive the standard equation of a plane. This transition from 'a flat surface' to 'the set of all vectors orthogonal to a specific direction' is the most important concept of the day. It transforms the equation from a static picture into a dynamic vector relationship, which is exactly the mindset needed for the upcoming sessions on column spaces and projections.

tasks: Sketch the intersection of two planes in 3D.
Write the equation of a 3D plane given a normal vector and a point.
Explain why three planes in 3D might not have a common intersection point.

sessions.title: Column Space and the Geometry of Ax = b
sessions.description: This session reinterprets the matrix equation Ax=b as a question of whether b is in the column space of A. You will learn to see matrix-vector multiplication as a 'recipe' for combining columns, which is a foundational perspective for modern data science and the upcoming unit on transformations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by challenging the traditional 'row-picture' view of matrix-vector multiplication that students often bring from high school. Instead of focusing on dot products and arithmetic, I will introduce the 'Column Picture' of the equation Ax = b. On the whiteboard, I’ll write a matrix A with two columns, v1 and v2, and multiply it by a vector [x1; x2]. The core pedagogical move here is to visualize this not as a calculation, but as a 'recipe.' I’ll explain that x1 and x2 are simply instructions—weights telling us how much of each column to grab. This shifts the focus from 'solving for x' to 'building b' using the available columns as building blocks.

Next, I will formalize the concept of the Column Space, or C(A). I’ll draw two vectors in a 3D coordinate system (representing a 3x2 matrix) and show that their linear combinations trace out a 2D plane through the origin. This is the moment to emphasize the definition of Span: the Column Space is exactly the set of all possible vectors b that we can reach by mixing the columns of A. To make this intuitive, I’ll use the analogy of a chemical mixture; the columns are our base ingredients, and we are trying to find if we can mix them to achieve the specific 'flavor' of vector b. If b lies on that plane, a solution exists; if it hovers above it, the system is impossible. This visualization prevents the common misconception that any 3-dimensional b can be solved by a matrix with three rows; students often forget that the number of columns (the available directions) is what actually limits our reach.

To solidify this, I’ll conduct a quick mental practice task. I’ll present a matrix where the columns are clearly multiples of each other (e.g., [1, 2] and [2, 4]) and ask the class what its column space looks like in 2D. The realization that it’s just a line—despite having two columns—is a crucial 'aha' moment for understanding linear dependence. This leads directly into the relationship between the existence of a solution and the size of the span. I will explain that 'solving' Ax=b is equivalent to asking: 'Is b inside the shadow cast by the columns of A?'

Finally, we will address the case of the 'Impossible System.' I will draw a 3D diagram where the Column Space is a 2D sheet and vector b points sharply away from it. This provides a geometric reason for why Gaussian elimination fails (yielding a 0=1 contradiction). I’ll explain that in these cases, the target vector b has a component that is 'outside the universe' of A. This sets the stage for future discussions on projections and least squares, as students will naturally start wondering: 'If we can't reach b exactly, what is the closest point on the plane we can get to?' I’ll conclude by reiterating that the column space represents the total 'reach' or 'capability' of the matrix, a perspective that is essential for understanding Rank and the Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra later in the course.

tasks: Explain the relationship between the existence of a solution and the span of matrix columns.
Identify the column space of a 3x2 matrix.
Draw a diagram showing a vector b that is not in the column space of A.

sessions.title: Null Space and Homogeneous Systems
sessions.description: This session focuses on the set of all vectors that are mapped to zero, known as the null space. You will learn how to find the null space by solving Ax=0, which represents the 'lost' or 'redundant' dimensions in a linear mapping process.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from 'where can Ax reach?' (Column Space) to 'what does A collapse to nothing?'. I will start by drawing a standard 3D coordinate system on the board and introducing the concept of the 'Null Space' as a secret room within the domain. The central hook for this lecture is that the Null Space (N(A)) represents the loss of information—it is the set of all input vectors x that the matrix A crushes into the zero vector. I will emphasize that while Ax=b is about reaching a target, Ax=0 is about exploring the internal 'blind spots' of the matrix itself.

To bridge the gap from intuition to calculation, I’ll write a 3x3 matrix on the board that has linearly dependent columns—perhaps one column is a multiple of another. I will frame the search for the Null Space as solving the homogeneous system Ax=0. This is the moment to explain that the zero vector is always a 'trivial' solution, but our true goal is to find if there are any non-zero vectors that A 'kills'. This leads naturally into performing Gaussian elimination. I will highlight that the 'Free Variables' identified in the reduced row echelon form (RREF) are the actual architects of the Null Space; they represent the degrees of freedom we have to move around without changing the output from zero.

Once we have the RREF, I will demonstrate how to express the pivot variables in terms of the free variables. This is a critical pedagogical step where learners often get lost in the algebra. I will explicitly show how to 'factor out' the free variables to write the solution as a linear combination of vectors. This allows me to define the 'Basis for the Null Space.' I'll explain that these vectors are the fundamental directions of redundancy. If the Null Space is a line, it means any movement along that line in the input space is completely ignored by the matrix. I will use the term 'kernel' as a synonym here, connecting the linear algebra concept to the broader mathematical idea of a function's kernel.

To reinforce the geometry, we will look at a 3x3 matrix of Rank 2. I’ll explain that if the rank is 2, the matrix is essentially 'collapsing' 3D space onto a 2D plane. Therefore, one dimension must be lost. I will ask the students to visualize this lost dimension as a line passing through the origin. This line is the Null Space. I’ll warn them about a common misconception: that the Null Space is 'nothing' because it maps to zero. On the contrary, the Null Space is a physical subspace—a line or a plane in the input space—that exists before the transformation even occurs.

We will conclude with a practice moment where I ask the learners to relate the number of free variables directly to the dimension of the Null Space (the Nullity). I’ll pose a challenge: 'If a 10x10 matrix has 10 pivots, what does the Null Space look like?' The realization that it must be just the origin (the zero vector) is a 'lightbulb moment' that confirms they understand the inverse relationship between information preserved (Rank) and information lost (Nullity). This sets the perfect stage for our final session on how these 'blind spots' shift the solutions of non-homogeneous systems.

tasks: Find the basis for the null space of a given matrix.
Relate the number of free variables to the dimension of the null space.
Describe the null space of a 3x3 matrix of rank 2 geometrically.

sessions.title: Structure of the General Solution
sessions.description: This session explains how the general solution to Ax=b is composed of a particular solution plus the null space. You will learn the 'geometry of translation', seeing how a solution set is a shifted version of the null space, completing your understanding of linear system structures.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the final mystery of the linear system $Ax=b$: if we know how to find a single solution and we know how to find the null space, how do they combine? I will start by writing a specific example on the board, perhaps $x + y = 3$. Students immediately recognize this as a line. I'll then contrast it with $x + y = 0$, which is the parallel line through the origin (the null space). The central theme of this session is that the 'b' in the equation doesn't change the shape of the solution space; it only changes its location. I will frame the 'particular solution' ($x_p$) as an anchor point that drags the entire null space away from the origin.

To derive the general form $x = x_p + x_n$, I will lead the class through a simple but profound subtraction. If we have two different solutions to $Ax=b$, say $u$ and $v$, what happens when we subtract them? By distributing $A(u-v) = Au - Av = b - b = 0$, we reveal that the difference between any two solutions must live in the null space. This is the 'aha' moment: it proves that every possible solution is just our one particular solution plus some 'wiggle room' defined by the null space. I will emphasize that $x_p$ is just one specific 'zip code' that gets us into the solution neighborhood, while $x_n$ describes all the possible streets we can walk down within that neighborhood.

Moving to visualization, I will draw a 3D coordinate system. If the null space is a plane through the origin, $Ax=b$ becomes a parallel 'flat' plane floating elsewhere in space. I will use this to address a common misconception: students often think that if there are infinite solutions, they can be 'anything.' I will correct this by showing that even with infinite solutions, they are strictly constrained to this shifted plane. This is where I'll introduce the practice task regarding why we can't have exactly two solutions. If we have two points in our solution set, the entire line segment (and the infinite line through them) must also satisfy the equation due to this linear structure. There is no middle ground between one solution and infinity.

Finally, I will walk through the procedural decomposition using a concrete matrix example. We will use Gaussian elimination to find the general solution in parametric form. I will show the students how to literally 'read' the particular solution from the constants and the null space from the coefficients of the free variables. This decomposition is vital because it separates the 'fixed' requirement of the system from its 'redundancy.' I will conclude by previewing how this 'particular + homogeneous' structure isn't just a matrix trick—it's the exact same logic they will later encounter in differential equations, reinforcing the idea that linear algebra provides the universal grammar for mathematical systems.

tasks: Decompose a given solution into particular and homogeneous parts.
Visualize the solution set of Ax=b as a line or plane shifted away from the origin.
Explain why Ax=b cannot have exactly two solutions.

projects.deliverable_increment: A Document-Term Matrix (DTM) representing the corpus as a collection of column vectors.
