units.title: Matrices and Linear Transformations
units.description: Shift focus from solving static equations to understanding dynamic transformations. This unit frames matrices as functions that map vectors from one space to another, highlighting the structural properties of these maps through rank, nullity, and matrix algebra.

lectures.title: Matrix Algebra
lectures.description: This lecture establishes the rules of matrix operations, moving beyond simple arithmetic to understand how these structures interact and how matrix multiplication represents the composition of linear processes.

sessions.title: Matrix Addition, Scaling, and Multiplication
sessions.description: This session introduces the formal arithmetic of matrices, covering element-wise addition, scalar multiplication, and the dot-product definition of matrix multiplication. You will gain the ability to perform these computations reliably and identify when certain operations are undefined. Mastering these mechanics is essential for the practical application of linear algebra in data science and engineering.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the operational foundation of linear algebra. While we often think of matrices as static grids of numbers, we are now going to treat them as active objects capable of being combined, scaled, and combined. We begin by defining the matrix not just as a table, but as a structured entity where shape dictates possibility. I will start by drawing two matrices of different dimensions on the board to pose a fundamental question: when is it mathematically 'legal' to combine these? This leads naturally into matrix addition and scalar multiplication. The core idea here is component-wise consistency. I will emphasize that for addition, the matrices must be identical in 'real estate'—same rows, same columns—because we are essentially merging corresponding pieces of information. To ground this, I’ll use a simple inventory example where two matrices represent stock in different warehouses; adding them represents the total business state.

Next, we shift to scalar multiplication. This is the 'volume knob' of matrix algebra. I’ll demonstrate how multiplying a matrix by a single real number—say, -2—is an act of uniform scaling that affects every entry simultaneously. A critical pedagogical moment here is addressing the common pitfall where students confuse scalar multiplication (which hits every element) with row operations from previous units (which might only hit one row). I will draw a clear distinction: scalar multiplication is a global property of the matrix object itself. I’ll prompt the learners to visualize a 2x2 matrix as a rectangle on a coordinate plane; scaling the matrix is equivalent to stretching or shrinking that entire shape. This prepares them for the transition from arithmetic to transformation.

We then move to the most significant mechanic of the session: matrix multiplication. I will avoid the 'row-by-column' mantra at first and instead frame it as a series of dot products. On the whiteboard, I will use a high-contrast color to trace the horizontal movement across the first matrix's rows and the vertical movement down the second matrix's columns. The most important concept to convey is the 'Inner Dimension Rule.' I will write out the dimensions of two matrices, such as (2x3) and (3x2), and circle the inner '3s' to show that they must match for the 'gears' of multiplication to mesh. If they don't match, the operation is physically impossible. This visual check prevents the common error of trying to multiply matrices that are dimensionally incompatible.

To solidify this, I’ll walk through a full 2x3 by 3x2 calculation step-by-step. I will narrate the 'walk and fall' motion: walking across the row while falling down the column. After the calculation, I will pause to point out that the resulting matrix has dimensions of the 'outer' numbers (2x2). This isn't just a rule to memorize; it represents how information is filtered through a system. I'll ask the students to consider why a 3x2 matrix multiplied by a 2x3 matrix would result in a much larger 3x3 output. This realization—that the order and shape of matrices fundamentally change the scale of the result—serves as the perfect cliffhanger for our next session on why matrix multiplication is not commutative.

tasks: Compute the product of a 2x3 and a 3x2 matrix.
Determine if two given matrices can be added based on their dimensions.
Scale a matrix by a factor of -2 and add it to another matrix.

sessions.title: Matrix Multiplication as Composition
sessions.description: This session explores the deeper meaning of matrix multiplication, explaining why it is non-commutative and how it represents the sequential application of two functions. You will understand how to view the product AB as applying transformation B followed by transformation A, which is a core intuition for complex systems. This perspective shifts your goal from rote calculation to conceptual mastery of linear pipelines.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by challenging the standard arithmetic intuition that multiplication is just 'repeated addition' or a commutative property where order doesn't matter. In matrix algebra, we must pivot from seeing a matrix as a static grid of numbers to seeing it as a dynamic action—a function that takes a vector and moves it to a new location. Explain that if matrix B is a function g(x) and matrix A is a function f(x), then the product AB is the composition f(g(x)). This is the single most important conceptual bridge: we read matrix multiplication from right to left, just like function notation, because the vector hits the matrix on the right first.

To visualize this, use a concrete geometric example on the whiteboard. Sketch a simple square in a 2D coordinate system. Define matrix B as a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation and matrix A as a horizontal shear or a scaling along the x-axis. Walk through the physical process: first, the square rotates (Action B), then the rotated square is stretched (Action A). Now, pose the critical question: what happens if we swap the order? If we stretch first and then rotate, the final position of the square's corners will be entirely different. This visual disparity provides the 'aha' moment for why AB is not equal to BA, grounding a dry algebraic rule in physical reality.

Address the common misconception that matrix multiplication is element-wise. Students often want to multiply A[1,1] by B[1,1] because addition worked that way. Correct this by returning to the 'dot product' mechanic but framing it as 'rows of the first meeting columns of the second.' Explain that each entry in the resulting matrix is the result of a specific 'pathway'—a row from the first matrix (representing the output dimensions of the final transformation) interacting with a column from the second (representing the input basis vectors). If the dimensions don't line up, it’s because the output of the first process isn't a valid input for the second process; the 'pipeline' is broken.

Introduce a brief practice moment where you provide two matrices—one that scales and one that reflects—and ask the students to predict the result of applying them in different orders before doing the math. This reveals whether they are thinking about the transformation or just crunching numbers. Use this to lead into the final segment on 'linear pipelines.' Explain that in fields like computer graphics or data processing, we often multiply dozens of matrices together to form one 'Master Matrix.' This Master Matrix represents a complex sequence of events—rotation, translation, projection—distilled into a single grid of numbers. This efficiency is why we bother with the complexity of matrix multiplication in the first place.

tasks: Explain why AB is not usually equal to BA using a geometric example.
Given two transformation matrices, find the single matrix that performs both actions in sequence.
Identify the dimensions of an output vector when a matrix is applied to a specific input.

sessions.title: The Identity and Matrix Inverses
sessions.description: This session defines the identity matrix as the 'one' of matrix algebra and introduces the concept of an inverse as a way to undo a transformation. You will learn the conditions under which a matrix is invertible and how the inverse relates to the original map's reversibility. This provides a critical tool for solving equations of the form Ax=b by isolating the vector x.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a parallel between simple numeric algebra and matrix algebra to establish the need for an identity element. Just as the number 1 satisfies the property 1 * x = x for any number, we require a matrix structure that leaves vectors and other matrices unchanged. Draw the Identity matrix (I) for 2x2 and 3x3 cases on the whiteboard, highlighting the '1's on the main diagonal and '0's elsewhere. Explain that this represents a transformation that 'does nothing'—it doesn't rotate, scale, or shear the space. This is a crucial conceptual anchor: if we want to isolate a variable in an equation like Ax = b, we need a way to turn A into I.

Transition into the concept of the Matrix Inverse by framing it as 'undoing' a transformation. If a matrix A rotates a vector by 90 degrees, its inverse A⁻¹ must rotate it back by 90 degrees. Write the formal definition AA⁻¹ = I and A⁻¹A = I. It is vital to emphasize that not every matrix has an inverse. Use the geometric analogy of 'collapsing' space; if a matrix squashes a 2D plane onto a 1D line, information is lost forever, and no inverse can 'reconstruct' that lost dimension. This helps prevent the common misconception that any non-zero matrix must be invertible.

Introduce the Determinant for a 2x2 matrix as a diagnostic tool for invertibility. Show the formula ad - bc and explain that this value represents the scaling factor of area. If the area becomes zero, the matrix is singular (non-invertible). This provides learners with a concrete computational check before they attempt complex inversions. Walk through a quick example where the determinant is zero to show the 'algebraic crash' that occurs when trying to divide by zero in the inverse formula, linking arithmetic intuition to matrix mechanics.

Conclude by demonstrating how the inverse allows us to solve the linear system Ax = b. Show the step-by-step symbolic manipulation: multiplying both sides by A⁻¹ from the left to yield x = A⁻¹b. Warn the students that while this is conceptually beautiful for isolation, it requires A to be 'square' and 'non-singular.' This session sets the stage for the Gauss-Jordan method by establishing exactly why we are hunting for that inverse: it is the 'undo button' that unlocks the value of our unknown vectors.

tasks: Verify if a given 2x2 matrix is the inverse of another by multiplication.
Calculate the determinant of a 2x2 matrix to check for invertibility.
State the properties of the identity matrix in various dimensions.

sessions.title: Elementary Matrices and Computing Inverses
sessions.description: This session connects row operations to matrix multiplication by introducing elementary matrices and the Gauss-Jordan method for finding inverses. You will be able to construct an inverse matrix systematically by augmenting with the identity and performing row reduction. This bridge between algebraic rules and computational algorithms is a major milestone in your technical proficiency.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the manual labor of Gaussian elimination and the formal structure of matrix algebra. The core realization to share with the audience is that every 'action' we perform on a system of equations—scaling a row, swapping rows, or adding a multiple of one row to another—can be encapsulated as a standalone matrix itself. I will start on the whiteboard by writing a simple 3x3 identity matrix and then performing a single row operation on it, such as swapping Row 1 and Row 2. This result is our first Elementary Matrix. The pivotal moment comes when we demonstrate that multiplying a matrix A by this Elementary Matrix E from the left (EA) produces exactly the same result as performing that row operation directly on A. This shifts the learner's perspective from seeing row reduction as a 'procedure' to seeing it as a series of 'transformations' or 'functions' applied to a matrix.

Next, I will lead the derivation of the inverse using this new language. If a matrix A can be reduced to the identity matrix I through a sequence of elementary row operations, then there exists a sequence of elementary matrices (E_k...E_1) such that their product with A equals I. This is the 'Aha!' moment for the Gauss-Jordan method: if those same operations are applied to the identity matrix simultaneously, we aren't just 'tracking' the steps; we are constructing the inverse matrix itself. I'll visualize this on the board by setting up the augmented [A | I] matrix. It is crucial to explain that the vertical bar is not just a separator, but a mirror reflecting the transformation of A into I on the left, and the birth of A-inverse on the right.

To solidify this, we will walk through a 3x3 inversion example. I will intentionally choose a matrix where the first step involves a row swap to highlight the 'Permutation' elementary matrix, and then use a scaling step. A common misconception for learners here is thinking that the order of operations doesn't matter or that they can perform column operations; I must emphasize that because we are pre-multiplying (EA), only row operations preserve the relationship we are building. I will pause here for a practice moment: asking the learners to write down the specific elementary matrix that represents 'adding 3 times Row 1 to Row 3.' This reveals whether they understand where the '3' goes in the identity grid and why it doesn't affect other rows.

Finally, we will conclude by discussing the 'Product of Elementary Matrices' theorem. If A is invertible, A can be written as the product of these elementary matrices. This is a powerful conceptual bridge because it suggests that complex matrices are actually built from very simple, atomic building blocks. I will illustrate this by taking the inverse of the operations we used to reduce A and showing how they 'reconstruct' the original matrix. This session isn't just about the mechanics of the [A | I] algorithm; it’s about proving that the inverse exists because we can decompose the matrix into a sequence of reversible, elementary steps.

tasks: Represent a row swap operation as an elementary matrix.
Use the [A | I] augmentation method to find the inverse of a 3x3 matrix.
Express a matrix as a product of elementary matrices.

lectures.title: Linear Transformations
lectures.description: In this lecture, we transition from viewing matrices as arrays of numbers to viewing them as dynamic operators that map one vector space to another, preserving the structure of the space.

sessions.title: What Makes a Map Linear
sessions.description: This session covers the two fundamental properties of linear transformations: additivity and homogeneity. You will learn to distinguish between linear and non-linear maps by testing these axioms. Understanding these requirements is vital for identifying which real-world phenomena can be modeled using the tools of linear algebra.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to a pivotal moment in our journey. Up until now, we have treated matrices as static grids—essentially spreadsheets of numbers. Today, we shift our perspective to see them as 'verbs' rather than 'nouns.' A linear transformation is a rule that moves vectors from one place to another while respecting the grid lines of space. Before we get into the math, I want to plant a visual seed: imagine a grid on a sheet of rubber. A linear transformation is a stretch, a rotation, or a flip that keeps the origin fixed and keeps all grid lines straight and parallel. If the grid lines curve or the origin moves, the 'linearity' is broken. This intuition is what we are about to formalize.

We define a transformation as 'linear' if it satisfies two ironclad rules: Additivity and Homogeneity. First, let's look at Additivity. I will demonstrate on the board that if you add two vectors and then transform the result, it must be the same as transforming them individually and then adding them. Why does this matter? Because it tells us that the 'sum of the parts' is the 'part of the sums.' Next, we tackle Homogeneity, or scaling. If I double the input vector, the output vector must also double. I’ll use a simple diagram to show that these two properties combined mean that the transformation preserves the basic operations of a vector space. If you can scale and add without breaking the mapping, you have a predictable, linear system.

To make this concrete, let's test a function like f(x,y) = (x+y, x). I will walk through the algebraic 'litmus test' on the whiteboard. We will plug in generic vectors (u + v) and compare the output. A common pitfall for students here is getting lost in the notation; I will emphasize that 'f' is just a machine, and we are checking if the machine treats a 'combo-meal' of vectors the same way it treats 'individual orders.' We’ll see that this specific function passes the test because the variables are only raised to the power of one and aren't multiplied together. This leads us to a crucial realization: linearity is about maintaining the 'flatness' and 'proportionality' of space.

Next, I’ll pose a trick question: Is a simple shift—a translation where we add a constant vector to everything—a linear transformation? On the surface, it looks simple, but when we test it against our two rules, it fails. I will show that f(x) = x + b (where b is not zero) fails homogeneity. If you double x, you don't double the output because that constant 'b' stays the same. This is a vital 'aha' moment: in linear algebra, 'linear' does not just mean a straight line in the sense of high school algebra (y=mx+b); it means a line that must pass through the origin. This leads us to our first theorem: any truly linear map must send the zero vector to the zero vector. If the origin moves, the transformation is 'affine,' not linear.

We conclude by reinforcing why these strict rules are the bedrock of the entire course. Because linear maps are so predictable, if we know what a transformation does to just a few 'basis' vectors, we can predict what it does to every single vector in the entire infinite space. This 'economy of information' is the secret power of linear algebra. I’ll leave the class with a challenge: think of a transformation like 'squaring every coordinate' and visualize why that would warp our rubber grid into a curve, failing our tests. This prepares them for the next session where we turn these abstract rules into the concrete language of matrices.

tasks: Test if the function f(x,y) = (x+y, x) is linear.
Explain why a translation (shifting) is not a linear transformation.
Prove that any linear map must send the zero vector to the zero vector.

sessions.title: The Matrix of a Linear Transformation
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to find the unique matrix that represents any linear transformation by observing where the standard basis vectors land. You will acquire the skill to translate geometric descriptions (like rotation or scaling) into numerical matrices. This ability to move between geometry and algebra is a primary goal for any linear algebra student.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by pivoting from the abstract rules of linearity to a concrete, visual realization: that every linear transformation is secretly just a matrix. To start this 'concept-first' lecture, I will draw the standard basis vectors, i-hat and j-hat, as the 'DNA' of the 2D plane. The central intuition to hammer home is that if you know where these two little unit vectors land after a transformation, you know where everything else lands. This is the 'tracking' principle—by following the unit vectors, we can map the entire grid. I'll sketch a grid being warped and show how any vector (x, y) is just a linear combination of these basis vectors, which explains why the transformation's behavior is entirely determined by its action on the basis.

Next, we will translate a geometric description—a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation—into numbers. I’ll show i-hat (1,0) rotating to (0,1) and j-hat (0,1) rotating to (-1,0). This leads us to the construction of the matrix by simply placing these landing spots as the columns of our matrix. It is crucial to address a common misconception here: students often try to put the vectors into rows. I will emphasize that the columns are the 'images' of the basis vectors, and this vertical arrangement is what allows the matrix-vector multiplication to work correctly as a weighted sum of those columns.

We then move to the concept of projection, specifically projecting vectors onto the x-axis. This is a great example of a transformation that 'squashes' dimension. I will visually demonstrate how i-hat stays where it is (it’s already on the x-axis), while j-hat is crushed down to the zero vector. The resulting matrix, with a column of (1,0) and a column of (0,0), helps students see that matrices aren't just for movement; they can be for information loss. This connects back to the idea of transformations being functions that can transform a 2D space into a 1D line.

To wrap up, I will pose a challenge: if we define a transformation where i-hat goes to (2,3) and j-hat goes to (1,-1), what happens to the vector (2,1)? This serves as a practical test of the session’s core logic. Instead of just plugging numbers into a formula, I'll encourage the class to think of it as '2 units of the first landing spot plus 1 unit of the second.' This reinforces the conceptual link between basis mappings and the algebra of matrix multiplication, ensuring they see matrices not as boxes of numbers, but as dynamic instructions for how space is being reshaped.

tasks: Find the matrix for a 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation in R2.
Construct a matrix that projects all vectors onto the x-axis.
Determine the image of a vector under a transformation defined by its basis mappings.

sessions.title: Kernel and Image
sessions.description: This session introduces the kernel (null space) and the image (column space) of a linear transformation, representing the 'inputs that go to zero' and the 'reachable outputs.' You will learn to calculate these subspaces, which provide deep insight into the information lost or preserved by a transformation. This is essential for understanding the solvability and uniqueness of linear systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by reframing the matrix not as a static table, but as a machine that processes space. The 'Kernel' and 'Image' are the two most fundamental ways to describe the character of this machine. To start, I will illustrate the concept of 'loss' in a transformation. I’ll pose a question: if you shine a flashlight on a 3D object and create a 2D shadow, what happened to the depth information? That 'lost' dimension is our entry point into the Kernel. I will define the Kernel (or Null Space) formally as the set of all input vectors that the transformation squashes into the zero vector. It’s crucial to emphasize here that the Kernel is a subset of the domain; it represents the 'blind spots' of the transformation where different inputs become indistinguishable at the output.

Transitioning to the 'Image' (or Column Space), I will shift the focus from what is lost to what is achieved. If the Kernel is about the 'hidden' inputs, the Image is about the 'reachable' outputs. I will visualize this by taking a 3D space and applying a transformation that flattens everything onto a specific plane. The plane itself is the Image. The core pedagogical goal here is to help learners see that the Image is spanned by the columns of the matrix—each column tells us where a standard basis vector lands. If those landing spots are redundant (linearly dependent), the Image 'shrinks' in dimension compared to the original space. This sets the stage for understanding why some systems of equations have no solutions: if your target vector isn't in the Image, the machine simply can't get you there.

Next, we will walk through the calculation of a basis for the Kernel using a 3x4 matrix. This is where the mechanics of Gaussian elimination meet the theory of subspaces. I will demonstrate that solving Ax = 0 is exactly how we identify the Kernel. A common pitfall for students is confusing the free variables with the Kernel itself; I will explicitly show how we use those free variables to parameterize the solution set, forming the basis vectors. We’ll pause for an exercise where students find the basis for a given matrix. This isn't just a calculation check; it's a diagnostic to see if they realize that the number of basis vectors in the Kernel corresponds directly to the 'missing' dimensions of the transformation.

To wrap up, I will connect these two spaces to the concept of 'information integrity.' If the Kernel contains only the zero vector, the transformation is 'one-to-one'—no information is collapsed or lost. If the Image covers the entire codomain, the transformation is 'onto.' I will use the example of a 3D space collapsing into a 2D plane to ask: 'Can we ever perfectly reverse this?' By showing that multiple points in the domain map to the same point in the 2D plane (the Kernel), students will intuitively grasp why we can't 'un-flatten' the space without losing the original coordinates. This prepares them for the Rank-Nullity Theorem by establishing the trade-off: the more you squash into the Kernel, the less space you have left for your Image.

tasks: Find a basis for the kernel of a given 3x4 matrix.
Describe the image of a transformation that collapses a 3D space into a 2D plane.
Determine if a specific vector is in the image of a transformation.

sessions.title: The Rank-Nullity Theorem
sessions.description: This session presents one of the most important balancing acts in linear algebra: the relationship between the dimension of the domain, the rank, and the nullity. You will learn to use this theorem to predict the behavior of linear maps without performing exhaustive calculations. This mastery allows you to verify the consistency of your results in complex problems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by framing linear transformations as a conservation law. Much like energy in physics, 'dimension' is a finite resource that a transformation must account for. I will start by drawing a large circle representing the domain and a smaller circle for the codomain. The central question is: when we apply a transformation, where does the 'stuff' go? This leads naturally to the introduction of the Rank-Nullity Theorem as a fundamental balancing act. I will emphasize that every dimension in the starting space must either be preserved (Rank) or collapsed to zero (Nullity). This concept-first approach prevents learners from seeing it as just another formula and instead as an accounting system for information.

To derive the logic, I will use a visual of a 3D space being projected onto a 2D plane. I'll ask the students to imagine a physical object being flattened. If the 'shadow' (the Image) is a 2D area, then one dimension must have been 'crushed' into the vertical direction (the Kernel). This sets the stage for the formal equation: Rank(A) + Nullity(A) = n. I will be very specific that 'n' is the number of columns, or the dimension of the domain, which is a common point of confusion for beginners who often try to use the number of rows. I'll explain that the domain is the 'source of potential,' and the theorem tells us how that potential is partitioned.

Next, we will apply this to a 5x7 matrix example to test the intuition. By telling the students the rank is 3, I'll prompt them to find the nullity. The goal here isn't the subtraction—which is trivial—but the interpretation: if we have 7 dimensions of input and only 3 dimensions of output, we have a 4-dimensional 'dead zone' where information is lost forever. This is a perfect moment to introduce the concepts of 'one-to-one' (injective) and 'onto' (surjective) transformations. I will explain that for a map to be one-to-one, the nullity must be zero—there can be no 'hiding' in the kernel. For it to be onto, the rank must equal the dimension of the codomain. I'll use the Rank-Nullity Theorem to show why a transformation from a smaller space to a larger space can never be 'onto,' and a transformation from a larger space to a smaller space can never be 'one-to-one.'

To wrap up, I will address a common misconception: the idea that rank and nullity are independent. I will demonstrate through a quick series of mental 'what-ifs'—if I increase the rank of a fixed-size matrix, the nullity must decrease. This trade-off is the 'DNA' of the matrix's behavior. We will conclude by revisiting previous exercises from the course, verifying that the dimensions of the subspaces we found manually always sum up to the number of columns. This provides a sense of mathematical closure and gives students a powerful 'sanity check' tool they can use in any future linear algebra problem.

tasks: Given the rank of a 5x7 matrix, find its nullity.
Explain what it means for a transformation to be one-to-one or onto using rank.
Apply the theorem to verify the dimensions of subspaces found in previous exercises.

lectures.title: Special Matrices
lectures.description: This lecture explores specific categories of matrices with unique properties, such as symmetry, orthogonality, and triangularity, which simplify computation and appear frequently in physics and data science.

sessions.title: Transpose and Symmetric Matrices
sessions.description: This session introduces the transpose operation and the concept of symmetry, where a matrix equals its transpose. You will learn why these matrices are ubiquitous in optimization and physical simulations. Recognizing these structures helps you choose more efficient algorithms for solving large-scale problems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the 'transpose' not as a dry algebraic rule, but as a change in perspective—literally flipping the grid. Start on the whiteboard by drawing a non-square matrix, perhaps a 3x2, and visualize the rows becoming columns. The core intuition to convey is that transposing swaps the roles of 'input dimensions' and 'output dimensions.' Instead of just showing the notation A^T, demonstrate how the element at index (i, j) migrates to (j, i). This movement is a symmetry across the main diagonal. It is vital to emphasize that for non-square matrices, the shape itself transforms (e.g., a tall matrix becomes a wide one), which has profound implications for how we view data tables where rows are observations and columns are features.

Next, we transition to the concept of the Symmetric Matrix, the 'perfection' of matrix forms where A equals its transpose. This is a critical pedagogical pivot: explain that symmetry isn't just an aesthetic property but a sign of deep internal balance. In the physical world, symmetric matrices often represent systems in equilibrium or distances between points. Use the whiteboard to write out a generic 3x3 symmetric matrix, highlighting how the off-diagonal entries mirror each other. Warn students about the common misconception that any matrix with 'matching numbers' is symmetric; clarify that the mirroring must happen strictly across the main diagonal, which acts as the 'spine' of the matrix.

To deepen the engagement, we move into a derivation phase to prove that the product of any matrix A and its transpose (AA^T or A^TA) is always symmetric. This is a 'magic' moment in linear algebra. Walk through the proof by applying the transpose rule (AB)^T = B^TA^T. Showing that (AA^T)^T equals AA^T itself reveals a foundational truth: even if a data set A is messy and non-square, its 'covariance-like' structures (A^TA) are inherently beautiful and symmetric. This step is essential because it prepares learners for optimization and the Normal Equations they will encounter later in the course.

We conclude by exploring the 'anatomy' of square matrices through the lens of symmetry and skew-symmetry. Introduce the idea that any square matrix can be decomposed into a symmetric part and a skew-symmetric part (where A^T = -A). Visualize this on the whiteboard as a mathematical 'orthogonality'—splitting a complex object into two simpler, fundamental components. This exercise serves as a diagnostic tool: if a student can successfully extract these components, they have mastered the mechanics of matrix addition and scalar multiplication alongside the transpose. End the session by hinting that these symmetric structures are the 'DNA' that makes the Spectral Theorem and SVD possible, grounding the abstract math in the course's ultimate goal.

tasks: Find the transpose of a non-square matrix.
Prove that the product of a matrix and its transpose is always symmetric.
Identify symmetric and skew-symmetric components of a square matrix.

sessions.title: Orthogonal Matrices and Rotations
sessions.description: This session focuses on orthogonal matrices, which represent transformations that preserve lengths and angles, such as rotations and reflections. You will understand the property that the transpose of an orthogonal matrix is its inverse. This is a foundational concept for computer graphics and high-dimensional data rotation.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the conceptual boundary between a 'static' matrix and a 'moving' transformation. Since the learner appreciates a concept-first public lecture style, frame the orthogonal matrix not as a list of numbers, but as a 'Rigid Body Motion.' Explain that in the vast universe of linear transformations, most matrices warp, stretch, or squash space, but orthogonal matrices are the elite guardians of geometry—they move the entire coordinate system while keeping every distance and every angle exactly as they were. This is the crucial 'DNA' of computer graphics: when you rotate a 3D model of a character, you aren't changing the character's shape, you are simply applying an orthogonal transformation.

Transition to the formal definition by visualizing the column vectors of a matrix. Explain that for a matrix to preserve the 'fabric' of space, its columns must be like the original basis vectors—unit length and perpendicular to each other. This is where the term 'orthonormal' should be introduced as the secret sauce of orthogonality. Draw out the dot product logic: if the columns are $u, v, w$, then $u \cdot u = 1$ (unit length) and $u \cdot v = 0$ (perpendicular). Use this to derive the most elegant property in linear algebra: $Q^T Q = I$. Show the class that the transpose of an orthogonal matrix isn't just a flip; it is the perfect undoing of the transformation. This bypasses the tedious Gauss-Jordan elimination entirely, providing a 'computational shortcut' that is the backbone of high-speed digital rotations.

Introduce the 2D Rotation Matrix as the primary specimen. Write out the $\cos(\theta)$ and $\sin(\theta)$ structure and walk through a 'mental check' of why it works. If we rotate by 30 degrees, we are essentially repositioning the x-axis and y-axis. Point out a common pitfall here: students often confuse a rotation with a reflection. Explain that while both preserve distances (and are both orthogonal), a reflection flips the 'handedness' of space (the determinant is -1), whereas a rotation preserves it (the determinant is +1). This distinction helps learners realize that orthogonality is a broad category containing different 'flavors' of motion.

Engage the learner with a verification exercise. Ask them to take a candidate 2x2 matrix and check two things: Are the columns length 1? Is their dot product 0? This task is designed to reveal that even if individual numbers look 'messy' (like $1/\sqrt{2}$), the underlying structure can be perfectly rigid. Follow this by proving the preservation of the dot product: if $(Qx) \cdot (Qy) = x \cdot y$, then the 'shadows' vectors cast on each other are invariant. This explains why orthogonal matrices are the standard for data rotation in PCA or SVD—they shift our perspective without distorting the data's internal relationships.

Conclude by reflecting on the efficiency of $Q^T = Q^{-1}$. In a world where inverting a matrix is usually the most expensive thing a computer does, orthogonal matrices offer a free lunch. Explicitly state that whenever they see a matrix whose columns look like an 'ideal' coordinate system, they should immediately look for the transpose to solve the system. This bridges the gap from abstract geometry to the practical 'numerical mastery' the course aims for, setting the stage for more complex factorizations like SVD later on.

tasks: Verify if a given 2x2 matrix is orthogonal.
Show that an orthogonal matrix preserves the dot product between vectors.
Calculate the inverse of a rotation matrix without using Gauss-Jordan.

sessions.title: Triangular and Diagonal Matrices
sessions.description: This session examines matrices that are mostly zeros—diagonal and triangular matrices—and explains why they are the 'ideal' forms for computation. You will learn how back-substitution makes triangular systems easy to solve. Understanding these forms prepares you for matrix factorization techniques covered later in the course.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the general complexity of matrices to the elegance of sparsity. Start the whiteboard session by drawing a standard 3x3 matrix filled with random numbers and contrast it with a 'Diagonal Matrix' where only the main diagonal is populated. The core idea to emphasize here is that diagonal matrices represent the simplest possible linear transformations—pure scaling. I will explain that if a matrix is the 'instruction manual' for space, a diagonal matrix is one where each axis is treated independently, avoiding any 'mixing' or shearing. This simplicity isn't just aesthetic; it is the computational gold standard we strive for in more advanced topics like Eigendecomposition.

Next, I will move to the mechanics of diagonal arithmetic, which often surprises learners with its intuitiveness. I'll demonstrate that multiplying two diagonal matrices is equivalent to simply multiplying their corresponding diagonal entries. This is a crucial moment to address a common pitfall: students often try to apply the full row-by-column dot product rule and get lost in the zeros. I will explicitly show how the zeros 'cancel out' the cross-terms, leading to the realization that the inverse of a diagonal matrix is just a matrix of the reciprocals of its entries. This provides a 'eureka' moment regarding why we want matrices in this form—it turns matrix algebra into simple scalar arithmetic.

Transitioning to 'Triangular Matrices', I will introduce the Upper (U) and Lower (L) forms. The visualization here is key: draw the 'staircase' boundary and explain that these matrices represent systems in a state of partial resolution. While diagonal matrices are perfectly decoupled, triangular matrices are 'ordered.' I will explain that in an upper triangular system, the last variable is already 'trapped' and solved, which leads naturally into the concept of Back-Substitution. This is the bridge to the next session on LU factorization, and I want to frame triangular matrices not as 'incomplete' but as 'structured for efficiency.'

To wrap up, I'll walk through a concrete example of solving $Ux = b$ using back-substitution on the whiteboard. I will narrate the process as a 'falling domino' effect: once we find the bottom-most variable, it unlocks the one above it, and so on. The important takeaway for the learner is that we don't need complex algorithms like Gauss-Jordan elimination once a matrix is in this form. This session concludes by framing these special matrices as the 'target destinations' for almost all numerical linear algebra—we take a messy, dense matrix and use clever tricks to reveal the diagonal or triangular skeleton hidden within.

tasks: Solve an upper-triangular system of equations using back-substitution.
Explain why the product of two diagonal matrices is diagonal.
Find the inverse of a non-singular diagonal matrix.

sessions.title: Block Matrices and the LU Factorization
sessions.description: This session introduces block matrix notation and the LU factorization, which decomposes a matrix into a product of a lower and an upper triangular matrix. You will learn how this decomposition accelerates solving the same system with different right-hand sides. This is a critical skill for anyone aiming for professional mastery in numerical linear algebra.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by introducing block matrices as a way to see the 'forest for the trees.' Explain that we can treat sub-sections of a matrix as if they were single scalars, provided the dimensions align. This is a crucial mental shift from element-wise thinking to structure-wise thinking. Illustrate this on the whiteboard by drawing a large square matrix divided into four quadrants (A, B, C, D) and show how the multiplication rule (AB + CD) mirrors the standard dot product but at a higher level of abstraction. This concept is the 'Lego-block' approach to linear algebra that makes handling massive datasets computationally feasible.

Transition from block notation to the core objective: the LU Factorization. Frame this not just as another algorithm, but as the underlying 'engine' of Gaussian elimination. Explain that while Gaussian elimination is a process of finding a solution, LU is the process of recording that solution's DNA. Draw a matrix A and visually separate it into L (a Lower triangular matrix representing the steps of elimination) and U (the Upper triangular matrix representing the final echelon form). The key intuition here is that we are 'unbaking the cake,' separating the operations we performed from the result we achieved.

Walk through the manual derivation of LU for a 3x3 matrix. Highlight the 'multipliers' used in each row operation and show how they populate the lower triangle (L), while the modified rows form the upper triangle (U). Address a common pitfall: students often forget that the diagonal of L is composed of 1s (the identity of our operations). Explain that if we keep track of our row operations in this way, we never have to perform the full elimination process from scratch ever again for the same matrix A, even if the result vector 'b' changes.

Introduce the 'Two-Step' solve method to demonstrate the practical power of LU. Show the logic chain: if Ax = b and A = LU, then L(Ux) = b. We define a temporary vector y = Ux and solve Ly = b first via 'forward substitution' (the easiest possible linear system). Once we have y, we solve Ux = y via 'back substitution.' Contrast this with the high cost of computing a full matrix inverse. Emphasize that in real-world scenarios, like structural engineering or weather modeling where 'A' is fixed but 'b' changes constantly, LU factorization is the professional standard for efficiency.

Conclude by having the students visualize the block-wise multiplication of L and U to reconstruct the original matrix A. This serves as the ultimate sanity check. Explain that mastering this decomposition is the first step toward understanding how modern software packages actually 'think' about linear systems, bridging the gap between classroom theory and numerical reality.

tasks: Multiply two matrices using block-wise partitions.
Perform an LU decomposition on a 3x3 matrix manually.
Solve Ax=b by first solving Ly=b and then Ux=y.

projects.stage_description: Implement a weighting transformation (such as TF-IDF scaling) as a matrix multiplication to adjust the importance of different terms within the vector space.
projects.deliverable_increment: A normalized and scaled Weight Matrix applied to the initial document vectors.

exams.title: Matrices and Linear Transformations Unit Exam
exams.goal: Evaluate the student's ability to manipulate matrices, interpret them as transformations, and use their properties to characterize linear maps.
sections: This comprehensive exam covers matrix algebra, the identity and inverse, properties of linear transformations (linearity, kernel, image, rank-nullity), and the characteristics of special matrices including LU decomposition.
successCriteria: Correctly compute matrix products and inverses.
Determine if a transformation is linear and find its standard matrix.
Calculate rank and nullity and verify the Rank-Nullity Theorem.

units.title: Determinants and Vector Spaces
units.description: Dive into the scaling factor of linear transformations—the determinant—and generalize our understanding to abstract vector spaces. This unit bridges the gap between concrete coordinate systems and the universal rules that govern any linear system.

lectures.title: Determinants
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the determinant, moving from its geometric interpretation as a signed volume scaling factor to the formal algebraic methods used to compute it for any square matrix.

sessions.title: Determinants as Signed Area and Volume
sessions.description: This session will teach you the geometric intuition behind the determinant as the factor by which a transformation scales areas in 2D and volumes in 3D. You will be able to visualize why a zero determinant implies a collapse of dimension and how the sign represents orientation. Mastering this concept provides the essential 'why' behind matrix invertibility, a core goal of your conceptual mastery.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a standard 1x1 unit square on the whiteboard, defined by the unit vectors i and j. This sets the stage for the 'concept-first' approach by establishing a baseline for area. The core objective is to shift the learner's perspective from a matrix as a table of numbers to a matrix as a 'stretching machine.' Ask the students to imagine this unit square being morphed as we apply a 2x2 matrix transformation. The fundamental question is: by what factor does the area of that square change? This factor is the determinant.

Introduce the 2x2 determinant formula not as an arbitrary rule, but as the area of the parallelogram formed by the columns of the matrix. Draw a parallelogram in a 2D coordinate system and show how the columns of the matrix represent the transformed unit vectors. Most learners struggle with why the formula (ad - bc) works; explain it visually by showing the larger rectangle containing the parallelogram and subtracting the outer triangles. Emphasize that if the area is 2, the transformation doubles the space; if it's 0.5, it shrinks it. This is the 'scaling factor' intuition that underpins all of linear algebra.

Transition to the concept of 'Zero Determinant' as a dimensional collapse. Use a whiteboard animation or a sequence of drawings to show a parallelogram getting flatter and flatter until its two side vectors are collinear (linear dependence). At this point, the area becomes zero. This is a critical pedagogical moment: explain that a zero determinant means the transformation has squashed the 2D plane into a 1D line (or a 0D point), losing information in the process. This is why a matrix with a determinant of zero isn't 'invertible'—you can't undo a collapse that has erased an entire dimension.

Introduce the concept of 'Orientation' to explain negative determinants. Imagine flipping a sheet of paper over; the area remains the same, but the relative positions of the vectors i and j have swapped. On the whiteboard, label the vectors to show a 'right-hand' versus 'left-hand' orientation. A negative determinant indicates that the space has been flipped or mirrored. This prevents the common misconception that area cannot be negative; in linear algebra, the 'signed' part of 'signed area' tells us about the structural integrity and orientation of the transformation.

Conclude the session by extending this intuition into 3D. Draw a unit cube and explain that for a 3x3 matrix, the determinant represents the volume of the 'parallelepiped' formed by the three column vectors. The logic remains identical: if the volume is zero, the 3D space has collapsed into a 2D plane or lower. Use the practice task of a transformation with a 0.5 determinant to check if learners understand that this applies to any shape within the space, not just the unit cube—if the 'grid' scales by 0.5, every object inside it scales by 0.5. This prepares them for the algebraic rigor of cofactor expansion in the next session by grounding it in a physical reality.

tasks: Calculate the area of a parallelogram defined by two 2D vectors using a 2x2 determinant.
Explain what happens to the volume of a cube under a transformation with a determinant of 0.5.

sessions.title: Computing Determinants by Cofactor Expansion
sessions.description: This session introduces the Laplace expansion method for calculating determinants of larger matrices using minors and cofactors. You will learn the recursive algorithm to break down complex matrices into manageable 2x2 calculations. This skill is vital for solving the characteristic equations you will encounter when we reach eigenvalues later in the course.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the intuitive, geometric 'scaling factor' concept from the previous session and the algebraic machinery needed to handle higher dimensions. While a 2x2 determinant represents the area of a parallelogram, we must now address how to calculate this value when the 'shape' exists in 3D, 4D, or beyond. I will introduce the concept of the 'Minor' not as a dry definition, but as a 'sub-view' of the matrix—explaining that to understand the whole, we must look at what remains when we systematically ignore one row and one column. This reductionist approach is the heart of the Laplace expansion, and I will emphasize that we are essentially breaking a complex problem into a hierarchy of simpler 2x2 problems.

The transition to 'Cofactors' introduces the chessboard pattern of signs (+, -, +, ...). This is a common friction point where students often ask 'why' the sign flips. I will explain this as an orientation tracker; just as reversing two vectors flips the sign of an area, moving through the matrix rows and columns toggles the orientation of the sub-spaces we are measuring. By visualizing a grid of alternating signs over the matrix, we transform the calculation from a series of random multiplications into a rhythmic, structured algorithm. I will demonstrate the first expansion on a 3x3 matrix, explicitly drawing the lines through the first row and first column to show the remaining 2x2 matrix, and then repeating the process across the top row to show the summation of these 'weighted areas'.

A critical tactical insight for this session is 'The Path of Least Resistance.' Rather than always expanding along the first row, I will teach the learners to scan the matrix for zeros. A zero in a matrix is a gift—it eliminates a term in the expansion entirely. This shifts the learner's mindset from mechanical calculation to strategic observation. We will practice an example where one column has two zeros and another has none, showing how choosing the 'sparse' column reduces a five-minute calculation to a thirty-second one. This reinforces the idea that in linear algebra, the structure of the data dictates the efficiency of the solution.

To conclude, we will address the recursive nature of this method. I will explain that while we are doing 3x3s today, this same logic allows us to tackle 10x10 matrices by breaking them into 9x9s, then 8x8s, and so on. This 'nested' logic is what computers use under the hood, and it provides the necessary algebraic foundation for finding Eigenvalues later in the course, where we will solve for variables hidden inside these very determinants. The final practice task will involve a 3x3 matrix with one carefully placed zero, challenging the student to identify the most efficient row/column to expand and successfully navigate the sign-toggling of cofactors.

tasks: Compute the determinant of a 3x3 matrix using cofactor expansion along the first row.
Choose the optimal row or column for expansion to minimize calculation steps.

sessions.title: Determinants and Row Operations
sessions.description: You will explore how elementary row operations—swapping, scaling, and adding rows—affect the value of a determinant. By learning these rules, you will be able to compute determinants of large matrices much faster than using cofactor expansion alone. This session connects your previous knowledge of Gaussian elimination to the properties of determinants, building a systematic understanding of matrix algebra.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by acknowledging the 'curse of dimensionality' in the cofactor expansion method introduced previously. While cofactor expansion is elegant, it becomes computationally impossible for large matrices. I will frame this session as a search for efficiency, bridging the gap between our geometric intuition of determinants and the mechanical power of Gaussian elimination. The goal is to show that we can 'clean up' a matrix using row operations to find its determinant almost instantly, provided we understand the tax—or the discount—each operation applies to the final value.

I will start the whiteboard by drawing a simple 2x2 identity matrix and its unit square area (determinant = 1). Then, I’ll demonstrate the first row operation: scaling a row. If we multiply a row by a constant 'k', we are effectively stretching the area along one dimension. I’ll explain that the determinant scales linearly with the row: det(kA) = k * det(A). A common trap for students is thinking that multiplying the entire matrix by k scales the determinant by k; I will use a 2x2 example to show that if you scale both rows, the area scales by k squared, emphasizing that the determinant 'sees' row operations one line at a time.

Next, we move to the row swap (permutation). Geometrically, this represents a flip in orientation—turning a right-handed coordinate system into a left-handed one. I will demonstrate that each single swap multiplies the determinant by -1. To ensure students grasp the cumulative effect, I'll pose a quick challenge: if we swap rows three times, what happens? This reveals if they understand that the 'sign' is a toggle; an odd number of swaps keeps the negative sign, while an even number returns us to the original orientation. This is crucial for later work with permutation matrices.

Then, we tackle the 'magic' operation: adding a multiple of one row to another. I will visualize this as a 'shear' transformation on our parallelogram. By drawing a rectangle and then shearing it into a slanted parallelogram with the same base and height, I can visually prove why this operation does not change the area—and thus, does not change the determinant. This is the most important realization of the session because it means we can perform Gaussian elimination to create zeros without worrying about altering the determinant's value. This justifies the entire strategy of reaching an upper triangular form.

Finally, I will combine these rules into a systematic workflow. I'll write a 4x4 matrix on the board and demonstrate the 'Triangular Path.' I’ll explain that for an upper triangular matrix, the determinant is simply the product of the diagonal entries, because all the 'shearing' and 'scaling' has simplified the volume into a hyper-rectangle. We will walk through a practice example where we use row replacements to zero out the lower triangle, keeping a careful 'ledger' on the side of the board of any row swaps or scaling factors used. This ledger approach prevents the common error of losing track of sign flips during a long calculation.

tasks: Convert a 4x4 matrix to upper triangular form and calculate its determinant by multiplying the diagonal elements.
Determine how the determinant changes when two rows are swapped three times.

sessions.title: Multiplicativity and Invertibility
sessions.description: This session covers the critical theorem that the determinant of a product is the product of the determinants, and its implication for matrix inverses. You will understand why a matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero. This serves as a definitive test for system consistency, directly supporting your goal of academic mastery in linear algebra.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between geometry and algebra. Having established that the determinant represents the 'scaling factor' of space, it is intuitive to ask: what happens if we apply two transformations in a row? If Matrix B scales space by a factor of 2, and Matrix A scales space by a factor of 3, then the combined transformation AB should scale space by a factor of 6. This leads us to the critical product rule: det(AB) = det(A)det(B). The teacher should start by sketching two linear maps on the board—first a shearing, then a scaling—and visually demonstrate that the total change in volume is simply the product of the individual changes. This sets the stage for a formal understanding of why multiplication of matrices behaves so elegantly with respect to the determinant.

From this foundation, we pivot to the concept of invertibility, which is the cornerstone of solving linear systems. A common pitfall for students is treating the determinant of an inverse matrix as a separate, complex calculation. By using the product rule on the equation AA⁻¹ = I, we can derive that det(A)det(A⁻¹) = det(I). Since the identity matrix doesn't scale space at all (its determinant is 1), it becomes immediately clear that det(A⁻¹) must be 1/det(A). This derivation is powerful because it transforms a symbolic manipulation into a logical necessity: if you expand space by 5, the only way to get back to the original size is to shrink it by 1/5.

This leads to the most important realization of the unit: the 'Zero Determinant' as a signal of non-invertibility. If the determinant of A is zero, it means the transformation has flattened space—collapsing a 2D plane into a 1D line or a 3D volume into a 2D sheet. Once information is lost in this collapse, there is no 'undo' button; no matrix can 'un-flatten' a line back into a plane. This is the geometric explanation for why a matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero. The teacher should emphasize that a zero determinant is a 'point of no return,' linking this back to the learner's goal of mastering system consistency.

To solidify these concepts, we introduce a practice moment where students calculate the determinants of two matrices and their product, then attempt to find the determinant of an inverse for a matrix with a determinant of zero. This task is designed to reveal a crucial misunderstanding: some students may try to apply the 1/det(A) formula even when det(A) is zero. Encountering the division by zero error serves as a visceral reminder that the inverse simply cannot exist in such cases. We conclude by framing the determinant not just as a number, but as a diagnostic tool that tells us whether a system of equations has a unique solution, no solution, or infinite solutions, providing the 'DNA' test for any square matrix.

tasks: Prove that if A is invertible, det(A inverse) = 1/det(A).
Check the invertibility of several matrices by evaluating their determinants.

lectures.title: Abstract Vector Spaces
lectures.description: In this lecture, we move beyond R^n to study the formal axioms that define a vector space, allowing linear algebra to be applied to polynomials, functions, and more.

sessions.title: Axioms of a Vector Space
sessions.description: This session will teach you the ten formal axioms that define a vector space, including closure under addition and scalar multiplication. You will gain the ability to recognize mathematical structures beyond arrows and numbers that behave like vectors. This transition to abstraction is necessary to apply linear algebra to advanced fields like differential equations or signal processing.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by challenging the traditional notion of what a 'vector' is. Up until now, students have likely visualized vectors as arrows in 2D or 3D space—concrete, geometric entities. The goal here is to shift the perspective to a 'concept-first' definition: a vector is anything that behaves like one. I will start by writing the two fundamental operations on the board—Addition and Scalar Multiplication—and ask the class why we were able to add functions in calculus or polynomials in algebra just as easily as we add arrows. This sets the stage for the formalization of these patterns into the ten axioms.

I will present the axioms not as a dry list to be memorized, but as the 'rules of the game' that ensure consistency. I'll group them logically: the 'Closure' axioms first, followed by the properties of addition (commutativity, associativity, identity, and inverse), and finally the scaling properties. The most important concept to emphasize is that if a set and its operations satisfy every single one of these rules, we can apply every theorem we’ve learned about linear systems and span to that set, no matter how 'un-vector-like' it looks. This is the power of abstraction: it allows us to solve differential equations using the same logic we use to find the intersection of two lines.

To solidify this, we will move to the first practice exercise: testing the set of all polynomials of degree exactly 2. This is a classic 'trap' for beginners. I will demonstrate that while adding two degree-2 polynomials often results in another degree-2 polynomial, it sometimes results in a degree-1 polynomial (e.g., (x^2 + x) + (-x^2 + 1) = x + 1). Because the degree is no longer exactly 2, we have 'fallen out' of the set. This reveals the crucial importance of the 'Closure' axiom—a vector space must be a closed universe. If an operation can take you outside the defined set, the structure collapses.

Next, we examine the set of integers under standard addition to address the requirement of scalar multiplication. While integers behave perfectly well under addition (they have an identity, 0, and inverses), they fail as a vector space because the 'scalars' in linear algebra are typically real numbers. If I take the integer '5' and multiply it by the scalar '0.5', the result is '2.5', which is not an integer. I will use this to explain that a vector space is always defined over a field (usually R), and if the set cannot handle scaling by any real number, it cannot be a vector space. 

I will conclude by summarizing that these axioms are a filter. Many mathematical objects pass through this filter—matrices, continuous functions, even solutions to certain differential equations. By the end of this session, students should feel that the term 'vector' is a job description rather than a physical definition. This pivot is essential because it prepares them for the next session on subspaces, where we will see how these rules help us identify smaller, perfectly formed universes within these larger abstract spaces.

tasks: Test if the set of all polynomials of degree 2 forms a vector space.
Identify which axiom is violated by the set of integers under standard addition.

sessions.title: Subspaces and Spanning Sets
sessions.description: You will learn the criteria for a subset of a vector space to be considered a subspace and how spanning sets describe these regions. You will be able to verify subspaces by checking zero vectors and closure properties. This session reinforces the geometric intuition of lines and planes within higher-dimensional abstract spaces.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by pivoting from the grand theory of vector space axioms to a more localized question: what if we only look at a subset of that space? To keep our 'concept-first' lecture style grounded, I will start by drawing a line through the origin in R^2. I want the students to see that this line is a 'universe' in its own right. If you add two vectors on that line, you stay on the line; if you scale a vector on that line, you stay on the line. This is the intuitive hook for a subspace—it is a subset that inherits the parent space's structure without breaking any rules. I will explicitly contrast this with a line that does *not* pass through the origin. By demonstrating how the zero vector is missing and how addition on such a line 'jumps' off the line, we solidify why the origin is the anchor of all linear algebra.

Next, I will formalize the 'Subspace Test' as a checklist for the students. Instead of checking all ten axioms from the previous session, we narrow it down to the big three: Does it contain the zero vector? Is it closed under addition? Is it closed under scalar multiplication? I'll explain that because the subset lives inside a valid vector space, we get most properties for free, and these three are the only 'stress tests' that could actually fail. I will use the example of the first quadrant in R^2 to illustrate a failure of closure under scalar multiplication—multiplying by a negative constant pushes us out of the quadrant. This helps learners realize that 'subspace' is a very restrictive and special status, not just any collection of vectors.

Then, we transition to the concept of a Spanning Set, which I like to call the 'recipe book' for a subspace. If we have a collection of vectors, the set of all possible linear combinations they can form is their span. I'll represent this on the board as a building process: start with one vector (a line), add a second non-parallel vector (a plane), and so on. The core pedagogical move here is to show that a subspace is often *defined* by its span. I will pose the question: 'If I give you three vectors in R^3, what is the smallest subspace that contains them?' This leads naturally to the realization that the span *is* that subspace. We will practice this by looking at the space of 2x2 symmetric matrices—a more abstract example—and identifying the 'building block' matrices that, when combined, can create any symmetric matrix in that set.

To wrap up, I will address the common misconception that 'span' and 'subspace' are different objects. I will clarify that 'span' is an action or a description, while 'subspace' is the resulting structure. I'll guide the students through a mental exercise: 'If I take a plane in R^3 that is shifted away from the origin, is it a subspace?' When they realize it fails the zero-vector test, I will show them how it can still be described by vectors, but not as a linear span of a basis starting from the origin. This distinction between 'affine spaces' and 'linear subspaces' is crucial for their future work in data science and optimization, ensuring they understand that in our world, everything must eventually relate back to that zero-point equilibrium.

tasks: Determine if a plane not passing through the origin is a subspace of R^3.
Find a spanning set for the space of symmetric 2x2 matrices.

sessions.title: Coordinates Relative to a Basis
sessions.description: This session explains how any vector can be uniquely represented as a coordinate vector once a basis is chosen. You will learn to translate between 'abstract' vectors and 'concrete' column vectors. This is a fundamental step in the course, enabling us to use matrix tools on abstract objects like functions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a conceptual bridge: the gap between the abstract world of general vector spaces (like polynomials or functions) and the concrete numerical world of R^n. The core insight for students here is that once we have fixed a basis, an abstract vector loses its 'mystique' and can be treated exactly like a list of numbers. I will frame this by comparing it to choosing a language or a unit of measurement; the object (the vector) stays the same, but the way we describe it depends entirely on the 'dictionary' (the basis) we agree upon.

To make this concrete, I will use the whiteboard to define the 'Coordinate Vector.' I’ll explain that if B = {v1, v2, ..., vn} is a basis for a vector space V, then for any vector x in V, there exists exactly one set of scalars c1, c2, ..., cn such that x = c1v1 + c2v2 + ... + cnvn. These scalars are what we call the coordinates. I will emphasize the word 'unique'—this is the most important idea because it guarantees that our numerical representation isn't ambiguous. If a student wonders why uniqueness matters, I'll explain that without it, a single point in space would have multiple 'addresses,' making calculations impossible.

Next, I will walk through a transition from geometry to algebra using a polynomial example. I'll write down the space P2 (polynomials of degree at most 2) and the standard basis {1, t, t^2}. I want to show that the polynomial p(t) = 4 + 3t - 2t^2 is just the column vector [4, 3, -2] in disguise. This is a pivotal moment because it strips away the 'function' nature of the polynomial and reveals its underlying linear structure. I will prompt the students to consider what happens if we change the order of the basis elements—revealing the common pitfall that coordinates are an ordered list; changing the basis order changes the vector representation even if the set of vectors is the same.

I will then introduce a practice task: finding the coordinate vector of a polynomial relative to the standard basis. This isn't just a calculation; it's a test of whether they understand that the 'basis' provides the slots and the 'coordinates' provide the weights. After this, we move to a more challenging scenario: R^2 with a non-standard basis. Here, I'll show that finding coordinates isn't always as simple as reading coefficients—it often requires solving a system of linear equations (the vector equation x = PB[x]B). I will visualize this on the board by drawing two different grids: the standard Cartesian grid and a 'skewed' grid formed by the new basis vectors.

To conclude, I will explain the 'Isomorphism' concept without necessarily using the intimidating term yet. I’ll describe it as a 'perfect mapping' where every operation in the abstract space (like adding two polynomials) has a perfect mirror image in the world of column vectors. This justifies everything we’ve done so far: we study matrices and R^n because, through the lens of coordinates, almost every finite-dimensional problem can be translated into that language. I’ll warn them that the 'magic' only works once the basis is fixed, setting the stage for the next session on what happens when we decide to switch those 'lenses' entirely.

tasks: Find the coordinate vector of a polynomial relative to the standard basis {1, x, x^2}.
Calculate the coordinates of a vector in R^2 relative to a non-standard basis.

sessions.title: Change of Basis
sessions.description: You will learn how to construct a change-of-basis matrix to convert coordinates from one system to another. You will understand how a single linear transformation can look different depending on the 'lens' (basis) through which it is viewed. This session prepares you for diagonalization in Unit 4, where choosing the right basis makes matrix powers simple.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the 'Change of Basis' not as a dry calculation, but as a translation between languages. Start the lecture by drawing a single vector on the whiteboard. Explain that while the 'physical' arrow doesn't change, the numbers we use to describe it depend entirely on our choice of grid—our basis. Introduce the scenario where one person sees the vector through the standard 'Euclidean' lens (Basis B), while another sees it through a customized, perhaps skewed lens (Basis C). This sets the conceptual stage: we aren't moving the vector; we are changing the observer's perspective.

To bridge from the previous session, demonstrate the construction of the Change of Basis matrix. The core logic to emphasize is that the columns of this transition matrix are simply the basis vectors of the 'old' system expressed in the coordinates of the 'new' system. Draw out the mapping: $v_C = P_{C \leftarrow B} v_B$. A common pitfall for students is getting the direction of the transformation backward. To combat this, use the 'identity' trick—show that the matrix is essentially an identity operator that maps the description from one coordinate system to another without altering the vector's identity. Use the whiteboard to physically align the columns of the matrix with the target basis to show how the scaling factors are redistributed.

The most important takeaway here is the concept of a 'Transformation under a Basis.' I will explain that linear maps like rotations or shears look simple in some bases and terrifyingly complex in others. Introduce the idea of 'Similarity'—the $A = PDP^{-1}$ structure—without using the term 'Diagonalization' too heavily yet. Show that to perform an operation in a difficult basis, we can 'translate' back to a friendly basis, do the math there, and 'translate' back. This 'sandwich' of matrices is the logical foundation for everything that follows in Unit 4 regarding eigenvalues.

During the practice phase, ask the students to compute a transition matrix from an orthonormal basis to a skewed one. This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand the 'cost' of non-orthogonality; they will see how the simplicity of projections disappears when the basis vectors aren't at right angles. I will conclude by teasing the upcoming project: explaining that in data compression, we change the basis to one where most coordinates are near zero, allowing us to 'throw away' unimportant information. This connects the abstract algebra to the practical goal of the image compressor they are building.

tasks: Compute the transition matrix from basis B to basis C.
Convert a vector's coordinates from an orthonormal basis to a skewed basis.

lectures.title: Applications of Determinants
lectures.description: This lecture concludes the unit by exploring how determinants are used to solve systems, find inverse formulas, and calculate the physical transformation of space.

sessions.title: Cramer's Rule
sessions.description: This session teaches Cramer's Rule, a method for solving linear systems using determinants. You will learn how to find individual variables in a system Ax=b without performing a full Gaussian elimination. This provides a clear algebraic alternative for small systems and deepens your understanding of how determinants relate to solution existence.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the first tactical application of our journey into determinants. To set the stage, we frame the problem of solving a linear system Ax = b. Until now, we’ve relied on Gaussian elimination—a robust, 'brute force' method that finds the entire solution vector at once. But today, we explore a surgical alternative: Cramer's Rule. The core intuition to convey is that a linear system can be viewed as an attempt to express the output vector b as a weighted sum of the columns of A. If we want to find just one specific coordinate of x, we can do so by measuring how much b 'contributes' to the total volume (determinant) relative to the original columns. This shift from 'solving a system' to 'comparing volumes' is the conceptual leap for today.

We begin the whiteboard derivation by visualizing a 2x2 matrix as two vectors forming a parallelogram. If we replace the first column of the matrix with the output vector b, we create a new parallelogram. Cramer’s Rule states that the value of the first variable, x₁, is simply the ratio of the area of this new 'mutated' parallelogram to the area of the original one. As I draw this, I will emphasize that this is a scaling relationship. If the determinant of A represents the 'total capacity' of the system, replacing a column with b tells us how much that specific column’s 'share' of the capacity is used to reach the target b. This visualization prevents the rule from feeling like a random algebraic recipe and anchors it in the geometry we’ve already established.

Moving to the algebraic formula, I will demonstrate how xᵢ = det(Aᵢ) / det(A), where Aᵢ is the matrix formed by replacing the i-th column with b. This is the moment to address the 'Efficiency Trap.' While Cramer's Rule is mathematically elegant, it is computationally expensive for large systems because calculating many high-order determinants is slower than row reduction. I will frame this as a tool for small, 2x2 or 3x3 systems, or for theoretical physics and engineering where we need a symbolic expression for a single variable without solving for the others. This distinction ensures learners know *when* to reach for this tool in their mathematical toolkit.

To solidify this, we will pause for a 2x2 practice example. I will present a system like 3x + 2y = 5 and x + 4y = 10. Instead of just doing the math, I will ask the learners to calculate det(A) first. This is a critical diagnostic step: if det(A) is zero, the 'volume' of the transformation is flat, and our ratio method breaks down because we cannot divide by zero. This naturally leads to the final discussion on the existence of solutions. If the determinant is zero, Cramer's Rule signals that the system is either inconsistent or has infinite solutions, reinforcing the determinant as a 'health check' for the invertibility of a system. By the end of this session, students should see Cramer's Rule not as a replacement for Gaussian elimination, but as a specialized diagnostic and surgical tool for linear systems.

tasks: Solve a 2x2 system of equations using Cramer's Rule.
Identify the conditions under which Cramer's Rule cannot be applied.

sessions.title: The Adjugate and the Inverse Formula
sessions.description: You will learn about the adjugate (adjoint) matrix and how it provides an explicit formula for the inverse of a matrix. You will be able to calculate matrix inverses for small matrices without row reduction. This theoretical tool is a staple of standard linear algebra mastery and helps in symbolic mathematical derivations.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the algorithmic world of Gaussian elimination to the elegant, symbolic world of the adjugate matrix. The core idea here is to bridge the gap between 'how' we find an inverse and 'what' an inverse is composed of algebraically. I will start on the whiteboard by revisiting the formula for a 2x2 inverse, which most students memorize as a trick—swapping the main diagonal and negating the off-diagonal. Today, we reveal that this 'trick' is actually a specific instance of a universal formula involving the adjugate. This shift is vital because it moves the learner from rote memorization to understanding the structural symmetry of matrices.

To construct the adjugate, we must first master the Matrix of Cofactors. I will demonstrate this using a 3x3 matrix, emphasizing that each entry in this new matrix represents the 'influence' of all other rows and columns. I'll describe the process of finding a cofactor as 'masking'—hiding the row and column of an element and calculating the remaining determinant.
