units.title: Orthogonality and Applications
units.description: Apply the principles of perpendicularity to solve real-world problems. This final unit covers inner products, orthogonal projections, and the powerful Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), providing the tools for data fitting and compression.

lectures.title: Inner Products and Orthogonality
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the formal geometry of vector spaces by defining how we measure lengths and angles, leading to the powerful concept of orthogonal projection.

sessions.title: Dot Products, Norms, and Angles
sessions.description: You will learn how to generalize the concept of a dot product to define the norm of a vector and the angle between vectors in any dimension. Understanding these measures allows you to quantify 'closeness' and 'direction' in data, which is foundational for all geometric algorithms in linear algebra.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the transition from the world of abstract vector spaces back to the intuitive world of geometry. While we have spent much time on spans and linear combinations, we now address a fundamental missing piece: measurement. Start by asking the audience how we know if two pieces of high-dimensional data are 'similar'. This sets the stage for the dot product not just as a matrix operation, but as the engine for measuring length and direction. On the whiteboard, draw two 2D vectors and define the dot product algebraically, then immediately bridge to the geometric interpretation. The most important idea here is that the dot product is a projection scaled by length; it tells us how much one vector 'echoes' in the direction of another.

Transition to the concept of the Norm (length). Derive the norm from the dot product using the Pythagorean theorem analogy. It is crucial to prevent the misconception that the norm is just a formula for 2D distance; emphasize that in high-dimensional spaces—like a 4D vector representing a customer profile—the norm represents the total magnitude of that data point. Use the whiteboard to show that the distance between two vectors is simply the norm of their difference. This shifts the learner's perspective from vectors as 'arrows' to vectors as 'points' in space, where the distance between points is a proxy for similarity.

Now, introduce the Law of Cosines to link the algebraic dot product to the cosine of the angle between vectors. This is the 'aha' moment where we show that the dot product encodes the relative orientation of two vectors. Highlight the sign of the dot product: positive means they point in the same general direction, zero means they are perfectly perpendicular (orthogonal), and negative means they point away from each other. This qualitative understanding is more important than the calculation itself. At this point, introduce the first practice task involving 4D vectors. This exercise is designed to prove that while we cannot visualize 4D space, the math provides a reliable 'geometric compass' that works in any dimension.

Finally, present the Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality. Rather than treating it as a dry theorem, frame it as a physical constraint: the shadow of a vector can never be longer than the vector itself. Write the inequality on the board and show how it guarantees that the cosine of an angle stays between -1 and 1. This provides the mathematical safety net for everything we do in geometry. Address a common pitfall where students forget that the inequality only reaches equality when vectors are linearly dependent (pointing in the same or opposite directions). Conclude by verifying this with a numerical example, ensuring the learners see that the math is consistent and sets the stage for defining 'orthogonality' as the ultimate form of independence in the next session.

tasks: Calculate the dot product and angle between two 4D vectors.
Verify the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for a given pair of vectors.

sessions.title: Orthogonal and Orthonormal Sets
sessions.description: This session covers the properties of vectors that are mutually perpendicular and have unit length. You will discover why orthonormal bases are the 'ideal' coordinate systems, simplifying complex projections into simple summations, which is a key step toward efficient computation in higher-level applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by pivoting from the dot product calculation to the geometric 'gold standard' of vector sets: orthogonality. I will start on the whiteboard by drawing a standard x-y Cartesian grid and asking the audience to consider why we find it so intuitive. The answer lies in the fact that the axes are perpendicular (orthogonal) and the units are uniform (normalized). This sets the stage for defining an orthogonal set as a collection of vectors where every distinct pair has a dot product of zero. I'll emphasize that this isn't just about 90-degree angles in a drawing; it is a structural guarantee that each vector in the set contains zero information about the others, representing a perfectly 'clean' coordinate system.

Next, I will derive the condition for an orthonormal set. It’s crucial here to bridge the gap between 'orthogonal' and 'orthonormal' by explaining that while orthogonality handles the direction, orthonormality handles the scale. On the board, I'll demonstrate the process of normalization—dividing a vector by its magnitude—to transform a set of perpendicular vectors into a set of unit vectors. I will explicitly address the common misconception that any set of independent vectors is 'good enough' for a basis; I'll explain that while any basis can span a space, orthonormal bases are the only ones that allow us to calculate coordinates as simple projections rather than solving complex systems of equations.

To solidify this, I'll introduce a practice moment where we check a set of three vectors in R3 for orthogonality. The goal here is to show that a single non-zero dot product 'breaks' the set’s special status. We will then take a successful orthogonal set and normalize it. I’ll point out that if the dot product of two vectors is zero, they are linearly independent by default—a powerful theorem that I’ll sketch out visually to show that you cannot build one perpendicular vector out of a combination of others. This 'independence for free' is the primary reward for seeking out orthogonal sets in higher dimensions.

Finally, I will conclude by showing the 'magic' of orthonormal bases in computation. I'll write out the identity matrix and point out that its columns are the simplest possible orthonormal set. I will explain that when we work with orthonormal vectors, the matrix transpose acts as the inverse, which is a massive computational shortcut. I’ll frame this as the ultimate 'efficiency' upgrade for linear algebra: by choosing the right coordinate system (orthonormal), we turn hard division problems into simple multiplication problems. This prepares the students for the next session on orthogonal complements, as they now have the tools to define what it means to be truly 'outside' or 'away from' a specific subspace.

tasks: Check if a set of three vectors is orthogonal or orthonormal.
Normalize a set of orthogonal vectors to create an orthonormal set.

sessions.title: Orthogonal Complements
sessions.description: We explore the relationship between a subspace and the set of all vectors perpendicular to it. Learning about orthogonal complements will help you decompose spaces into 'what we know' and 'what is left over,' a concept critical for understanding the fundamental subspaces of a matrix.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by positioning the concept of the 'orthogonal complement' as the geometric version of a 'missing piece' in a puzzle. Use the whiteboard to draw a subspace $V$ (like a line through the origin in $\mathbb{R}^2$) and pose the question: 'If this line represents everything we currently know, what is the set of all vectors that are completely independent of this knowledge in a geometric sense?' This leads naturally to the definition of $V^{\perp}$ (V-perp). Emphasize that being 'perpendicular to the subspace' doesn't just mean being perpendicular to one vector, but to every single vector within that span. This is the 'strongest' form of independence possible in linear algebra.

Transition to the formal notation and the 'Link to the Nullspace.' Draw a matrix $A$ and remind the audience of the relationship between rows and the nullspace. Explain that the Nullspace of $A$ is effectively the orthogonal complement of the Row Space. This is a critical pedagogical pivot: it transforms the abstract definition of $V^{\perp}$ into a practical computation problem. If a student wants to find $V^{\perp}$, they simply need to treat the basis vectors of $V$ as the rows of a matrix and solve for the nullspace using Gaussian elimination. This connects Unit 1 (systems of equations) to Unit 5 (geometry), showing that solving $Ax=0$ was always about finding vectors perpendicular to the rows.

Address the common misconception that the orthogonal complement is just 'any' other subspace. Use a 3D visualization of a plane (a 2D subspace) in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Show that while there are infinitely many lines not contained in the plane, only one line is 'orthogonal' to it. This is the moment to introduce the concept of 'Space Decomposition.' Explain the intuition that $V$ and $V^{\perp}$ together account for the entire dimension of the original space ($\mathbb{R}^n$). If $V$ is a plane ($n=2$), then $V^{\perp}$ must be a line ($n=1$) because $2+1=3$. This 'completeness' is why we call it a 'complement'—it fills in the dimensions that $V$ ignores.

Lead into a derivation/proof moment regarding the intersection of these spaces. Ask the students: 'Can a non-zero vector live in both $V$ and $V^{\perp}$ simultaneously?' Guide them through the logic: if a vector $x$ is in $V^{\perp}$, it must be perpendicular to every vector in $V$. If $x$ is also in $V$, it must be perpendicular to itself ($x · x = 0$). Since the only vector with a length of zero is the zero vector, the intersection must be trivial. This proof is essential because it guarantees that when we decompose a vector into 'what we know' and 'what is left over' in the next session, there is no ambiguity or overlap between the two parts.

Conclude by setting up the practice task. Have the students find the basis for the orthogonal complement of a plane in $\mathbb{R}^3$ defined by $x + 2y - z = 0$. This forces them to identify the normal vector as the basis for the complement. This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand that the coefficients of a plane's equation are actually the components of the vector that spans the orthogonal complement, bridging the gap between algebraic equations and geometric orthogonality.

tasks: Find the basis for the orthogonal complement of a plane in R3.
Prove that the intersection of a subspace and its orthogonal complement is the zero vector.

sessions.title: Orthogonal Projections
sessions.description: You will learn the mathematical process of 'shadowing' a vector onto a subspace. This session provides the geometric intuition and the formula for the projection matrix, which is the essential bridge to solving problems where an exact solution does not exist.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the problem through the lens of a 'best approximation.' In the real world, we often encounter systems of equations that have no solution—physical measurements that don't perfectly align or data points that don't fit a model. I will start the whiteboard by drawing a vector 'b' hovering above a plane 'W'. The core question is: if we cannot reach 'b' using the vectors in 'W', what is the closest we can get? I'll use the 'shadow' analogy here, explaining that the closest point must be the one where the error—the distance between the target and our approximation—is minimized. This happens when the error vector is perpendicular to the entire subspace.

To derive the formula for projecting a vector 'y' onto a line 'L' spanned by 'u', I will show that the projection is some scalar multiple 'c' of 'u'. The critical insight to emphasize is the orthogonality condition: (y - cu) must be orthogonal to 'u'. By setting their dot product to zero, we algebraically 'unlock' the formula for 'c'. I will pause here to address a common misconception: students often forget to divide by the dot product of 'u' with itself, assuming the direction vector is already normalized. I'll demonstrate how this scalar 'c' acts as a 'coordinate' for the projection in the 1D space of the line.

Moving from a line to a general subspace 'W', the complexity increases but the logic remains identical. If 'A' is a matrix whose columns form a basis for 'W', then the projection 'p' is equal to 'A' times some coefficient vector 'x-hat'. The most important derivation of this session is the 'Normal Equations'. I will show that for the error vector (b - Ax-hat) to be orthogonal to the column space of 'A', it must lie in the null space of A-transpose. This leads us to the beautiful equation: (A^T A) x-hat = A^T b. I'll explain that this isn't just a formula; it's a bridge that converts a 'broken' unsolvable system into a solvable one by collapsing the problem into the space we actually have access to.

Next, I will formalize the 'Projection Matrix' itself. By isolating 'p' in our derivation, we arrive at P = A(A^T A)^-1 A^T. This is a high-level conceptual pivot: I want the learners to see 'P' not as a collection of numbers, but as a geometric operator—a machine that takes any vector in the universe and smashes it down onto the subspace 'W'. I'll illustrate a 'sanity check' for the students: if we apply the projection matrix twice, nothing should change (P squared equals P). This reinforces the intuition that once a shadow is cast, casting a shadow of that shadow doesn't move it further.

To conclude, we will work through a practice task where we project a 3D vector onto a plane. This serves two purposes: first, to practice the matrix multiplication mechanics, and second, to verify that the resulting error vector is indeed orthogonal to the plane's basis vectors. This 'verification step' is vital; it transforms the math from a black-box calculation into a tangible geometric reality. I will end the session by hinting at the next major application: Least Squares regression, where this exact 'shadow' logic allows us to find the line of best fit for scattered data points.

tasks: Compute the projection of a vector onto a line and a plane.
Construct a projection matrix for a given subspace.

lectures.title: Orthogonal Bases
lectures.description: This lecture moves from theory to practice, providing the algorithms needed to construct orthogonal systems and solve overdetermined real-world problems.

sessions.title: The Gram-Schmidt Process
sessions.description: This session teaches you the step-by-step algorithm to transform any basis into an orthogonal one. Mastering this process is vital because it allows you to 'straighten out' messy data into a clean, perpendicular coordinate system used in numerical software.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to one of the most mechanically satisfying yet conceptually deep sessions in the course. We begin by acknowledging a fundamental problem in data science and geometry: the 'curse of the slanted basis.' While any set of linearly independent vectors can form a basis, working with them is often a nightmare because changing one coordinate affects others. I will start the whiteboard by drawing two non-orthogonal vectors in R2 and trying to project a point onto them. The messiness of the algebra here serves as the 'why'—it justifies the need for the Gram-Schmidt process, which effectively 'rectifies' these vectors into a clean, perpendicular grid without losing the space they span.

The core of the Gram-Schmidt process is a recursive subtraction of 'shadows.' I will introduce the first vector, v1, as our 'anchor'—it defines the first direction, u1. To find the second direction, u2, we take the original vector v2 and subtract its projection onto u1. On the whiteboard, I will visualize this as taking a tilted vector and removing its horizontal component, leaving only the perfectly vertical piece. It is critical to emphasize here that we are not changing the space; we are just carving out a better perspective of it. A common misconception for learners is forgetting that we must subtract projections onto all *previously* found orthogonal vectors, not just the one immediately prior. I will highlight this by writing the formula for u3, showing two distinct subtraction terms to drive home the cumulative nature of the algorithm.

Once the algebraic steps are laid out, we will move into a 'live derivation' of a 3D example. This is where we apply the steps to a specific set of three vectors. I will narrate the process as 'clearing the path.' For the first vector, there is no interference. For the second, we remove the interference from the first. For the third, we remove the interference from both the first and the second. I will pause to ask: 'What happens if we started with a set that wasn't linearly independent?' This prompts the learners to realize that one of our resulting vectors would become zero, effectively uncovering the redundancy in the data. This serves as a diagnostic check for their understanding of span and independence.

To wrap up, I will discuss normalization. While Gram-Schmidt gives us an orthogonal basis, numerical stability and standard conventions usually require an 'orthonormal' basis—where every vector has a length of one. I will demonstrate how to scale our newly minted u-vectors into e-vectors. The key takeaway for the learners should be that this process is the 'pre-processing' step of linear algebra; it takes raw, correlated features and turns them into a set of independent, non-overlapping building blocks that make every subsequent calculation, from QR decomposition to Least Squares, significantly easier. This sets the stage for the next session on matrix factorization.

tasks: Apply Gram-Schmidt to a set of three linearly independent vectors.
Identify the geometric interpretation of each subtraction step in the process.

sessions.title: QR Decomposition
sessions.description: You will learn how to factor a matrix into an orthogonal matrix Q and an upper triangular matrix R. This decomposition is a fundamental tool in numerical linear algebra that makes solving systems and finding eigenvalues more stable and efficient.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by framing QR Decomposition not as a new piece of math, but as the elegant bookkeeping of the Gram-Schmidt process we just mastered. The central concept is that if Gram-Schmidt turns a messy set of basis vectors into a nice set of orthonormal ones, then we must be able to describe the original vectors in terms of those new ones. I will draw a matrix A and explain that we are looking for a 'biography' of A, written in two parts: Q, which contains the 'purified' orthonormal directions, and R, which stores the instructions or recipes for how those directions reconstruct the original columns. This shift from 'process' to 'product' is the most critical pedagogical transition for students to make.

On the whiteboard, I will write the matrix equation A = QR. I’ll start with a 2x2 case to keep the geometry clear. I will show how the first column of A is simply a scaled version of the first column of Q, but the second column of A is a linear combination of both the first and second columns of Q. This is where the 'Upper Triangular' nature of R becomes intuitive rather than a definition to memorize. By writing out the inner product relationships, I will demonstrate that column j of A only ever depends on columns 1 through j of Q. This 'look-back only' dependency is what forces all entries below the diagonal in R to be zero. I'll pause here to ask: 'Could column 2 of A ever need a component of the future column 3 of Q?' to solidify the realization that the construction process itself dictates the matrix shape.

To address potential confusion regarding the actual values inside R, I will explicitly show that R is composed of the projections (dot products) we calculated during the Gram-Schmidt steps. This demystifies the matrix multiplication. I will perform a 2x2 decomposition live, showing that the diagonal elements of R are simply the lengths of the orthogonal vectors before we normalized them, and the off-diagonal element is the 'overlap' we subtracted out. This connects the abstract matrix algebra back to the physical act of 'straightening' vectors. I'll warn students that if they ever find a non-zero value below the diagonal of R, it means they’ve accidentally allowed a 'future' vector to influence a 'past' one, which breaks the logic of the incremental construction.

Finally, I will motivate the 'Why' by discussing numerical stability. In a public lecture style, I’ll explain that while the inverse of a matrix is often 'fragile' and sensitive to rounding errors, the matrix Q—being orthogonal—is incredibly 'sturdy' because it preserves lengths and angles. By decomposing A into Q and R, we turn a difficult system-solving problem into a simple back-substitution problem using R. We conclude by setting up a 3x3 example for the students to try, challenging them to find R by simply performing the dot products of the original columns of A with their newly found orthonormal vectors in Q, proving that they now possess a powerful way to factorize and simplify linear systems.

tasks: Perform a QR decomposition on a 2x2 and 3x3 matrix.
Explain why the R matrix is always upper triangular based on the Gram-Schmidt process.

sessions.title: Least Squares Problems
sessions.description: We address how to find the 'best fit' solution when Ax=b has no solution. You will be able to minimize the error between your model and your data, which is the heart of regression analysis in statistics and machine learning.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by confronting the reality of 'broken' mathematics: the inconsistent system. In most real-world scenarios, we have more data points than variables (an overdetermined system), which geometrically means the vector 'b' does not lie within the column space of matrix 'A'. I will start by drawing a 3D plane (the column space) and a vector 'b' sticking out of it like a flag at an angle. The core conceptual hook here is to admit that while we cannot reach 'b' exactly, we can find the closest possible point on that plane. This shifts the goal from solving Ax=b to minimizing the 'error'—the gap between what we have and what we want.

To bridge the gap between intuition and calculation, I will introduce the 'Projection' concept as the hero of the story. If we want to find the point in the column space that is closest to 'b', the error vector (the difference between 'b' and the prediction) must be perpendicular to every vector in the column space. I’ll visualize this 'shadow' of the vector b onto the subspace. This leads us directly to the Normal Equations: A-transpose * A * x-hat = A-transpose * b. I will emphasize that this isn't just a formula to memorize; it is the mathematical translation of the phrase 'the error is orthogonal to the subspace.' This is the 'DNA' of the solution.

A common pitfall for learners is feeling confused about why we multiply by A-transpose on both sides. I will explain this by showing that A-transpose 'crushes' the dimensions into a square system that we can actually solve. We’ll walk through the derivation on the whiteboard, showing how this transformation ensures that even if A was tall and skinny, the resulting system is square and solvable. This is a critical pedagogical pivot: we aren't changing the problem; we are projecting it into a manageable reality.

Now we move to a hands-on exercise: taking a simple 3x2 system where three points don't align on a single line. I’ll ask the learners to set up the Normal Equations. The goal here isn't just to get the numbers right, but to see that the product A-transpose * A is symmetric and (usually) invertible. This practice session is designed to reveal that even when there is no 'perfect' solution, there is always a 'best' solution. I will challenge them to consider what happens if the columns of A are linearly dependent—introducing the risk of a non-invertible A-transpose * A—which connects back to our earlier units on rank.

Finally, we will frame this entire process as the engine behind Linear Regression. I want to convey that every time a machine learning model 'fits' a line to data, it is essentially solving this exact projection problem in a higher dimension. We conclude by looking at the magnitude of the error vector. I'll explain that the smaller this length is, the better our model fits the truth. This sets the stage for the final session, where we transition from abstract equations to drawing actual lines through scattered data points.

tasks: Set up the normal equations for an inconsistent system.
Find the least-squares solution for a simple overdetermined 3x2 system.

sessions.title: Fitting Lines and Curves to Data
sessions.description: This session applies the least squares method to practical data fitting, such as finding the line of best fit for a set of points. This demonstrates the direct utility of linear algebra in predictive modeling and data science.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by grounding the abstract 'Least Squares' formula derived in the previous session into a concrete, visual reality: the best-fit line. I will start by drawing four scattered data points on the board that do not lie on a single line. The central pedagogical goal here is to shift the learner's perspective from 'solving an equation' to 'finding a balance.' I’ll explain that while we want to satisfy a system like Ax=b, the 'b' vector (our data) is sitting outside the column space of 'A' (our model). By drawing a line that misses the points but minimizes the vertical 'gaps,' we are physically representing the projection of the data onto the model's possibilities.

To build the matrix 'A,' I will show how each data point (x, y) generates one row of our system. The first column of 'A' will be filled with ones—representing the y-intercept—and the second column with the x-coordinates—representing the slope. A common misconception for learners is why we use a column of ones; I will clarify that we are essentially saying 'y equals some constant times 1 plus some slope times x.' By setting up this 4x2 matrix, we transform a geometric fitting problem into a standard linear algebra problem. I will then walk through the calculation of the Normal Equations (A-transpose A times our coefficients equals A-transpose b), emphasizing that this step effectively 'squashes' the overdetermined system into a manageable 2x2 system that we can solve for the optimal slope and intercept.

Once the linear fit is established, I will pose a challenge: What if the data follows a curve? I will draw a parabolic set of points to demonstrate that 'Linear' Algebra isn't restricted to straight lines; it is linear in the *coefficients*. To model a quadratic fit, I will show how to expand our matrix 'A' by adding a third column containing the squares of our x-coordinates. This is a pivotal moment in the session where I explain that the machinery—the Normal Equations and the projection logic—remains exactly the same regardless of whether we are fitting a line, a parabola, or a high-dimensional surface. This realization empowers learners to see the Least Squares method as a universal tool for data science.

Finally, we will conduct a 'sanity check' exercise. I will ask the learners to look at the resulting residuals—the differences between the actual y-values and our predicted y-values. We will verify that the sum of these errors (when weighted by the columns of A) is zero. This isn't just a calculation check; it’s a deep dive into the geometry of orthogonality. It proves that our error vector is truly perpendicular to our model's subspace. By the end of this session, the learner should not only be able to calculate a best-fit line for four points but also understand why the Normal Equations are the most stable way to extract signal from noise in any empirical dataset.

tasks: Calculate the best-fit line for 4 given data points.
Formulate a quadratic fit using the same matrix methods.

lectures.title: Singular Value Decomposition
lectures.description: The course culminates in the SVD, the most versatile matrix factorization that reveals the structural importance of different components within data.

sessions.title: Singular Values and the SVD
sessions.description: You will learn the formal definition of the SVD and how it generalizes diagonalization to any matrix, not just square ones. This provides you with the ultimate tool for matrix analysis, revealing the 'singular values' that rank the importance of different data dimensions.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the absolute peak of our linear algebra journey. Today, we tackle the Singular Value Decomposition, or SVD. I want to start by framing this not as a new, scary formula, but as the 'Grand Unified Theory' of matrix factorization. So far, we’ve looked at diagonalization, which is beautiful but fragile—it only works for square matrices that are 'nice' enough. The SVD is the solution to that limitation. It is the realization that every single matrix, regardless of its shape or whether it's invertible, can be broken down into three fundamental movements. I will begin on the whiteboard by writing the iconic equation A = UΣVᵀ, and we will treat this as a forensic breakdown of a transformation.

First, we must define the cast of characters. I’ll introduce the Sigma matrix first, as it contains the 'singular values.' These are the heart of the SVD. I’ll explain that while eigenvalues tell us how a transformation scales its special eigenvectors, singular values tell us how a matrix stretches space in general. It's crucial to emphasize that these values are always non-negative and are traditionally ordered from largest to smallest. This ordering is why the SVD is so powerful for data science; it's a built-in ranking system of 'importance.' I'll warn the students about a common trap: thinking that singular values are just eigenvalues. They aren't, though they are deeply related, and we’ll uncover that link by looking at the product of A-transpose and A.

Next, we'll dive into the derivation. This is where the 'whiteboard' style shines. I will show how we find the components. We start by looking at AᵀA. Because this product is always a symmetric, positive semi-definite matrix, it is guaranteed to have non-negative eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors. This is our 'aha!' moment. I’ll demonstrate that the square roots of these eigenvalues are exactly our singular values, and the eigenvectors of AᵀA become our 'right singular vectors' (the V matrix). Then, we’ll see how applying the matrix A to these vectors leads us to the 'left singular vectors' (the U matrix). By constructing it this way, we show that U and V are orthogonal matrices—meaning they represent pure rotations or reflections—while Sigma handles all the stretching.

To solidify this, I’ll walk through a concrete numerical example using a small, non-square 3x2 matrix. This is the first practice moment. We won't just calculate; we will interpret. As we find the values for U, Sigma, and V, I'll ask: 'What does the first singular value tell us about the dominance of the first column of U?' This helps students bridge the gap between abstract symbols and the 'weight' of information. I’ll explicitly address the potential confusion regarding the dimensions of these matrices, especially for non-square cases, by drawing the matrix blocks on the board to show how the shapes must align for the multiplication to hold.

Finally, we will conclude by discussing why this generalization matters. While diagonalization requires a basis of eigenvectors that might not exist or might not be orthogonal, the SVD provides us with two different orthonormal bases (one for the row space and one for the column space). I will frame this as the 'Swiss Army Knife' of linear algebra. We are preparing the ground for the next session's geometric visualization, so I’ll leave them with the thought: if every matrix is just a rotation, a stretch, and another rotation, then no transformation is truly 'messy'—it’s just a sequence of simple geometric steps.

tasks: Identify the components U, Sigma, and V for a simple matrix.
Relate singular values to the eigenvalues of A-transpose times A.

sessions.title: Geometry of the SVD
sessions.description: This session visualizes how a matrix maps a circle to an ellipse, breaking the transformation down into rotation, stretching, and another rotation. This intuition is crucial for understanding how information is transformed and preserved in complex systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by setting a high-level conceptual stage: if the SVD is the 'Grand Unified Theory' of matrix factorization, its geometry is the story of how space is rearranged. The core objective is to move beyond the abstract formula A = UΣVᵀ and visualize it as a three-step dance. I will start by drawing a unit circle on the whiteboard, representing a set of vectors with a magnitude of one. This circle represents our starting point in the domain. The central question to pose to the students is: 'What happens to this perfect circle when we multiply it by any arbitrary matrix A?' By framing it this way, we shift from algebraic manipulation to a morphological study of space.

Next, I will decompose the transformation process into its constituent parts, starting with the rightmost matrix Vᵀ. On the whiteboard, I’ll illustrate that Vᵀ is an orthogonal matrix, which geometrically corresponds to a rotation or reflection. I will show that while the circle doesn't change its shape, the 'basis' or the grid lines on which the circle sits are being rotated. It is crucial here to emphasize that Vᵀ aligns the 'input' directions—the principal directions of the data—with the coordinate axes. A common misconception for learners is thinking Vᵀ changes the data's scale; I will explicitly clarify that Vᵀ preserves lengths and angles, merely reorienting our perspective.

Then, we introduce the action of the diagonal matrix Σ (Sigma). This is the 'stretching' phase. On the board, I will draw the transformation of the rotated circle into an axis-aligned ellipse. Each singular value (σ₁, σ₂, ...) represents the length of the semi-axes of this ellipse. I will use this moment to link the algebra to the geometry: the largest singular value σ₁ dictates the direction of maximum 'information' or variance. If a singular value is zero, the circle collapses into a line or a point, which provides a perfect visual bridge to the concept of the rank of a matrix. This visual of stretching and collapsing is the most important part of the session because it explains why some dimensions in data are more 'important' than others.

Finally, we apply the matrix U. Like Vᵀ, U is a rotation, but it takes the axis-aligned ellipse we just created and rotates it into its final orientation in the output space. I will draw the final tilted ellipse on the board. This completes the logic chain: Rotation (Vᵀ) -> Stretching (Σ) -> Rotation (U). I will highlight that while Vᵀ picks the 'best' directions to look at the input, U picks the 'best' directions to describe the output. To solidify this, I will lead a sketching exercise where students are given a simple Σ and asked to draw the resulting ellipse, then determine how U and V might tilt that ellipse. This exercise aims to reveal if students understand that U and V define the 'where' (orientation) while Σ defines the 'what' (the scale and importance).

To wrap up, I will address the 'SVD vs. Eigen-decomposition' confusion. I’ll explain that while Eigen-decomposition is like finding the stable, 'unchanging' directions of a square transformation, SVD is about finding the 'optimal' directions for any transformation. I will use the visualization of the unit circle and ellipse to show that while eigenvectors might not exist or might not be orthogonal, the singular vectors (the columns of U and V) always provide an orthogonal frame that captures the transformation's geometry perfectly. This prepares them for the next session on low-rank approximation, as they can now 'see' why cutting out small singular values simply means ignoring the thinnest, least significant axes of the ellipse.

tasks: Sketch the transformation of a unit circle based on given singular values.
Describe the orientation of the principal axes using the U and V matrices.

sessions.title: Low-Rank Approximation
sessions.description: You will learn how to discard the least significant singular values to simplify a matrix while keeping its essential structure. This concept is the mathematical engine behind noise reduction and efficient data storage.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the central problem of data science: complexity vs. utility. Now that we have the SVD, we have a sorted list of 'importance' via the singular values. The key insight of this session is that we don't need the whole matrix to understand its story. I will start on the whiteboard by writing the SVD as a sum of rank-1 matrices: A = σ₁u₁v₁ᵀ + σ₂u₂v₂ᵀ + ... + σᵣuᵣvᵣᵀ. By visualizing these as layers of an image, I will show that the first few layers contain the 'bone structure' of the data, while the later layers are just the 'skin texture' or, more often, random noise. The most important idea here is that the Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem guarantees that truncation is not just a guess—it is the mathematically optimal way to simplify data.

To bridge the gap between abstract algebra and practical application, I will walk through the construction of a rank-1 approximation. I'll take a simple 2x2 matrix where one singular value is significantly larger than the other. I will explicitly draw out the outer product of the first singular vectors and multiply by the first singular value. The core pedagogical move here is to show that even though we've 'lost' information, the resulting matrix still captures the primary direction and scale of the original transformation. This prevents the common misconception that 'low-rank' means 'low-quality'; in many cases, a low-rank approximation is actually 'cleaner' because it filters out high-frequency noise that resides in the smaller singular values.

Next, we tackle the measurement of loss using the Frobenius norm. I will explain that the 'error' of our approximation isn't just a random number; it is precisely related to the singular values we chose to ignore. On the whiteboard, I'll derive why the square root of the sum of the squares of the omitted singular values equals the Frobenius norm of the difference between the original and the approximation. This is a critical moment for the learner to see that linear algebra allows us to quantify exactly how much 'truth' we lose when we compress data. I'll frame this as a 'budgeting' problem—how many singular values can we afford to keep for the project's data compression engine without losing the essence of the image?

I will conclude the session with a practice moment where learners must decide where to 'cut' the SVD for a hypothetical dataset. I'll present a list of singular values that drop off sharply after the third value. The task is to calculate the approximation error if we keep only two. This exercise is designed to reveal if the learner understands that the 'energy' or 'variance' of the data is concentrated in those top values. By the end of this session, the learner should view a matrix not as a static block of numbers, but as a prioritized stack of information where the most important signals always rise to the top.

tasks: Construct a rank-1 approximation of a rank-2 matrix.
Calculate the Frobenius norm error of a low-rank approximation.

sessions.title: Principal Components and Data Compression
sessions.description: This session connects the SVD to Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and image compression. By the end, you will understand how to reduce the dimensionality of large datasets, which is the final piece of your course project on building a data compression engine.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this final session by bridging the gap between abstract matrix factorization and the real-world noise of data. I’ll start on the whiteboard by drawing a 2D scatter plot of data points that form a stretched cloud. The core narrative here is that data is messy, but it usually has a 'preferred' direction. I will explain that the Singular Value Decomposition isn't just a math trick; it is a search for the axis where the data varies the most. This is the moment to connect the Sigma matrix from our previous session to the concept of 'Information Density.' I want to emphasize that the largest singular value corresponds to the direction of highest variance, effectively telling the learner that if they could only look at the data through one window, this is the window that captures the most story.

Next, I will transition into the mechanics of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) through the lens of SVD. Instead of treating PCA as a separate statistical entity, I will show how the matrix V contains the 'principal components'—the directions of the axes—while the singular values tell us the magnitude of importance for each axis. I’ll draw a diagram showing how we project high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace (like a line or a plane) and explain that the 'error' in our compression is simply the sum of the squares of the singular values we chose to ignore. The pedagogical goal here is to make the learner realize that dimensionality reduction is a conscious trade-off between simplicity and precision.

To solidify this, we will move into a mental walkthrough of image compression, which serves as the final milestone for the course project. I’ll describe an image not as a picture, but as a giant matrix of pixel intensities. I will illustrate how a rank-1 approximation—taking only the first column of U, the first singular value, and the first row of V-transpose—creates a ghost-like, blurry version of the image. By adding more layers (rank-2, rank-10, etc.), the image 'snaps' into focus. I’ll explicitly warn against the misconception that SVD is the most efficient way to store a JPEG in real life; rather, it is the most mathematically pure way to understand which features of the image are structurally dominant.

Finally, I will wrap up the session and the course by reflecting on the 'Total Energy' of a matrix. I’ll ask the learners to consider why we can throw away 90% of the singular values and still recognize a face in a compressed photo. This leads to the concluding insight: most data in the universe is redundant, and Linear Algebra is the tool we use to strip away that redundancy. I will prompt them to think about how this applies to their final project, ensuring they understand that the 'SVD engine' they are building is actually a filter for importance, allowing them to reconstruct complex signals from a handful of carefully chosen numbers.

tasks: Explain the relationship between variance and singular values.
Outline the steps to compress an image using the SVD.
